cards.title: Virtual Machines
cards.subtitle: AWS EC2 · Google Compute Engine · Azure VMs
cards.lego: The standard 2×4 rectangular brick: sturdy and fully customizable, but heavy. You own everything from the operating system up.
cards.summary: A hypervisor slices one physical server into isolated guests, each running its own kernel and operating system. You pick the CPU, memory, disk and image, and you are responsible for patching, configuring and scaling what runs inside.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: The software needs a full OS, a custom kernel module, GPUs, or licensed software tied to a machine.
You run long-lived, steady workloads where reserved or committed-use pricing beats paying per request.
You host your own databases, message brokers or Kubernetes worker nodes.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Boots in tens of seconds to minutes, so scaling reacts slowly to sudden spikes.
You patch the OS, rotate credentials and fight configuration drift between machines.
You pay for idle capacity unless an autoscaling group shrinks the fleet.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: The physical host fails and takes the VM with it. Spread instances across availability zones behind a load balancer.
Hand-patched 'pet' servers drift apart until one behaves differently in production. Build immutable images (Packer, AMIs) and replace instead of repair.
Noisy neighbours on shared hardware cause unpredictable latency.

sections.title: Remember
items: Classic trio: machine image + autoscaling group + load balancer with health checks.
Treat servers as cattle, not pets.

cards.title: Containers
cards.subtitle: Docker · containerd · OCI images
cards.lego: Uniformly sized modular bricks that stack perfectly on any baseplate, because each brick carries its own dependencies inside.
cards.summary: A container is an ordinary process isolated with Linux namespaces and limited with cgroups. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in about a second and packs densely. The image bundles the app with its libraries, so the same artifact runs on a laptop, in CI and in production.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: You deploy stateless web services and microservices.
You want 'works on my machine' to mean 'works everywhere', with the same image in development, CI and production.
You want to pack many small services onto fewer machines.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Isolation is weaker than a VM because every container shares one kernel.
One container is easy; hundreds need an orchestrator for placement, networking, secrets and rollouts.
State must live outside the container, in a database, cache or volume.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: The container restarts and its local disk is gone. Never keep the only copy of data inside it.
It is OOM-killed when it exceeds its memory limit, often in a restart loop.
Bloated images slow down every deploy and scale-out.

sections.title: Remember
items: Twelve-Factor rules: stateless processes, configuration in environment variables, logs to stdout.
Container = process + namespaces + cgroups + an image filesystem.

cards.title: Container Orchestration
cards.subtitle: Kubernetes · Amazon ECS · Nomad
cards.lego: The baseplate plus a robot that reads the instructions. You declare what the finished model should look like, and it keeps rebuilding it whenever a piece falls off.
cards.summary: You declare the desired state: which images, how many replicas, how much CPU and memory. Controllers keep reconciling reality toward it. They restart crashed pods, reschedule them off failed nodes, roll out new versions gradually, give services stable DNS names, and autoscale on metrics.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: You run many services that need rolling deploys, service discovery and autoscaling.
You want to use machines efficiently by bin-packing many workloads onto shared nodes.
You need one deployment model across clouds or on-premises.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Operating it is a job in itself: networking, upgrades, RBAC and YAML sprawl.
For one or two services, a managed platform or serverless is usually cheaper and simpler.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: A misconfigured liveness probe restarts healthy pods, which can cascade across the service.
Missing resource requests and limits cause noisy neighbours and surprise evictions.
A control-plane outage leaves running pods serving (static stability) but blocks deploys and scaling.

cards.title: Serverless Functions
cards.subtitle: AWS Lambda · Cloudflare Workers · Google Cloud Run functions
cards.lego: Tiny micro-bricks that appear the instant two pieces need connecting, then disappear. You never store or maintain them.
cards.summary: You upload a function and choose what triggers it: an HTTP request, a queue message, an object landing in S3, or a schedule. The platform runs one instance per concurrent event, scales to zero when idle, and bills per millisecond. Lambda isolates each function in a Firecracker microVM; Cloudflare Workers use V8 isolates, which start in under a millisecond at the edge.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Traffic is spiky or rare, so paying for idle servers is wasteful.
You need glue between managed services, such as 'image uploaded to S3, so resize it'.
Event handlers, webhooks, scheduled jobs and edge logic (redirects, auth checks, A/B tests).

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Cold starts: the first request to a new instance can take from about 100 ms to several seconds, depending on runtime and package size.
Hard limits: Lambda runs at most 15 minutes and has memory, payload and concurrency caps.
Functions are stateless, harder to debug locally, and tie you to the vendor.
At steady high load, per-request billing can cost more than containers.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: A traffic spike launches thousands of instances that exhaust the database's connections. Put a queue or a connection proxy (such as RDS Proxy) in between.
Asynchronous invocations are retried, so side effects can run twice. Make handlers idempotent.
Account concurrency limits throttle unrelated functions that share them.

cards.title: Relational Databases
cards.subtitle: PostgreSQL · MySQL · Amazon Aurora
cards.lego: The rigid LEGO grid: every piece must click into clean rows and columns, and nothing that doesn't fit is allowed on the board.
cards.summary: Data lives in tables with a fixed schema. You query it with SQL, joining tables as needed. Indexes (usually B-trees) keep lookups fast, and constraints such as foreign keys and uniqueness protect integrity. ACID transactions (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) make a group of writes all-or-nothing, even with many concurrent users.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Money, orders, inventory and bookings: anything where a half-applied change is a bug.
You need ad-hoc queries, reports and joins across entities.
The shape of the data is known and relationships matter. This is the default choice until proven otherwise.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Writes scale vertically until you add sharding (Vitess, Citus) or move to distributed SQL (Spanner, CockroachDB).
Schema migrations on big tables need care: online migrations, backfills and dual writes.
Read replicas scale reads but serve slightly stale data (replication lag).

sections.title: How it breaks
items: A burst of clients exhausts connections. Use a pooler such as PgBouncer and cap the size of the app's pool.
Hot rows, such as one inventory counter in a flash sale, serialize on locks.
A missing index turns a 1 ms lookup into a full table scan that drags down everything else.
Reading your own write from a lagging replica shows the user old data.

cards.title: NoSQL & Document Databases
cards.subtitle: DynamoDB · MongoDB · Cassandra · Bigtable
cards.lego: Flexible Bionicle pieces that morph into whatever shape you're storing, as long as you decide in advance how you'll pick them up.
cards.summary: There are four families: key-value (DynamoDB, Redis), document (MongoDB), wide-column (Cassandra, Bigtable) and graph (Neo4j). Most scale horizontally by hashing a partition key across many nodes and allow flexible, schema-on-read records. You model the data around your access patterns, not around entities, and usually denormalize.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: The scale is huge but access is simple and known: get by key, or a range inside one partition.
Write throughput is very high: messages, events, IoT readings, activity logs.
Records carry flexible, evolving attributes, such as product catalogs, user profiles, carts and sessions.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Joins and ad-hoc queries are weak or missing. Adding a new access pattern can mean a new index or a copy of the data.
Many are eventually consistent by default, and multi-item transactions are limited.
The partition key is the most important design decision and hard to change later.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: A hot partition, such as a celebrity's key or everything written under today's date, throttles while other nodes sit idle.
Full-table scans are slow and expensive.
Schema-on-read drift: old records in shapes the code no longer expects.

cards.title: Object Storage
cards.subtitle: Amazon S3 · Google Cloud Storage · Azure Blob Storage
cards.lego: Huge storage bins where you dump media, raw text and massive static assets. Each bin has a label, and you fetch things by label.
cards.summary: A flat namespace of buckets and keys, each pointing to an immutable blob plus metadata, accessed over HTTP. Capacity is effectively unlimited and cheap, and S3 is designed for 11 nines of durability. It is not a filesystem: you replace whole objects rather than editing them in place.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Images, video, audio, documents, backups, logs, ML datasets, a data lake.
Static website assets served through a CDN.
Any large blob: put the bytes in object storage and keep only the key and metadata in your database.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Each request takes tens of milliseconds, far slower than local disk or a cache.
You cannot edit part of an object; you rewrite it. Listing huge buckets is slow.
There are request-rate limits per key prefix, so spread hot keys across prefixes.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: A misconfigured public bucket leaks data. Block public access by default.
Routing uploads through your servers wastes bandwidth and CPU. Hand clients presigned URLs so they upload directly.
Event notifications are at-least-once, so the same upload may trigger processing twice. Consumers must be idempotent.

sections.title: Remember
items: S3 has provided strong read-after-write consistency since December 2020.
Lifecycle rules move old objects to cheaper tiers such as Glacier automatically.

cards.title: Wide-Column Stores: Cassandra
cards.subtitle: Apache Cassandra · ScyllaDB · Google Bigtable · HBase
cards.lego: A huge rack of labelled drawers spread over many tables. Every table can take new pieces at any moment, and each drawer keeps its pieces sorted.
cards.summary: A masterless, Dynamo-style cluster with a Bigtable-style data model. Rows are placed on a consistent-hash ring by partition key and replicated to N nodes (typically 3, across racks or zones). Any node can coordinate a request, and the consistency level is chosen per query (ONE, QUORUM, LOCAL_QUORUM, ALL). Writes go to a commit log and memtable and are flushed to immutable SSTables that are compacted later (an LSM tree), so writes are very fast. Inside a partition, rows are sorted by clustering columns, which makes 'latest N items for X' queries cheap.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Write-heavy, always-on workloads: messages, events, time series, activity feeds, IoT, audit logs.
Multi-datacenter active-active with local-quorum latency.
Access patterns are known up front: design one table per query.

sections.title: Data modeling rules
items: Primary key = (partition key, clustering columns…). The partition key spreads load; clustering columns sort rows inside it.
Bound partition size (roughly under 100 MB) by adding a time bucket to the key, for example (channel_id, day).
Denormalize: write the same data into several query-shaped tables. There are no joins.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: No joins, limited secondary indexes, and ad-hoc queries are expensive.
Lightweight transactions (Paxos-based compare-and-set) exist but are slow. Use them sparingly.
Repairs, compaction tuning, JVM garbage collection pauses (Cassandra) and tombstones take real operational care.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Hot or oversized partitions (a mega-channel or celebrity key) overload a few replicas.
Tombstone buildup from heavy deletes makes reads scan dead data and time out.
Skipped anti-entropy repair leaves replicas silently diverged, and deleted data can reappear.

sections.title: Similar blocks
items: ScyllaDB: Cassandra-compatible, rewritten in C++ with a shard-per-core design. Discord moved to it from Cassandra.
Google Bigtable and HBase: range-partitioned wide-column stores with a single master for metadata. Row-key design is the whole game.
Amazon DynamoDB: a managed service with similar partition and sort-key modeling.

cards.title: Distributed SQL (NewSQL)
cards.subtitle: Google Spanner · CockroachDB · YugabyteDB · Amazon Aurora
cards.lego: The rigid LEGO grid, but built from many baseplates snapped together, and it still feels like one board.
cards.summary: Relational databases that keep SQL and ACID transactions but scale out horizontally. Data is split into ranges or tablets, each replicated with Raft or Paxos, and transactions that span ranges use a distributed commit protocol. Spanner uses TrueTime for external consistency; CockroachDB and YugabyteDB use hybrid logical clocks. Aurora takes a different route: one writer, with a shared, replicated storage layer that scales reads and durability.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: You've outgrown a single Postgres or MySQL primary but still need transactions and SQL.
Multi-region deployments with strong consistency and automatic failover.
You want to avoid hand-rolled application-level sharding.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Every write pays for consensus. Cross-region transactions add tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
Hot ranges (sequential primary keys) still bottleneck. Use hashed or UUID keys.
Costs more and has more moving parts than a single-node database.

cards.title: Search Engines
cards.subtitle: Elasticsearch · OpenSearch · Apache Solr · Lucene
cards.lego: The index at the back of the instruction booklet: look up a word and it tells you every page it appears on.
cards.summary: Search engines build an inverted index (term → list of documents), plus BM25 relevance scoring, analyzers for tokenizing and stemming, facets and aggregations, and increasingly vector search too. An index is split into shards with replicas across nodes. It is fed from the source-of-truth database, usually asynchronously through change data capture or events, and is almost never the system of record.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Full-text product and catalog search, typeahead, log search and analytics, faceted filtering.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Near-real-time rather than instant: refresh intervals of about 1 s. Reindexing after a mapping change is costly.
The index drifts from the database if the update pipeline drops events. Plan full rebuilds.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Too many small shards overload the cluster state. Deep pagination and heavy aggregations exhaust memory.
Split-brain from bad quorum settings on older versions.

cards.title: Vector Databases
cards.subtitle: pgvector · Milvus · Vertex AI Vector Search · FAISS · Pinecone
cards.lego: A bin sorted by shape-similarity instead of by label: hold up a piece and it hands you the ones that look most like it.
cards.summary: Vector databases store embeddings (dense vectors from a model) and answer 'k nearest neighbours' queries with approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes. HNSW is a graph index: fast with high recall, but memory-hungry. IVF plus product quantization clusters and compresses vectors, so it is cheaper at billion scale. Metadata filters and hybrid search (combined with BM25) narrow the results. They are the retrieval brick behind RAG, semantic search, recommendations and deduplication.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for LLM apps, semantic or product search, similar-item recommendations.
Start with pgvector if you already run Postgres. Move to a dedicated engine for more than about 100 million vectors or very high QPS.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Recall vs latency vs memory is tuned through index parameters (HNSW M and efSearch, IVF nlist and nprobe).
Re-embedding the whole corpus when the embedding model changes is a batch job to plan for.

cards.title: Coordination Services
cards.subtitle: ZooKeeper · etcd · Consul · Google Chubby
cards.lego: The small, trusted referee's notebook that every builder checks to find out who's in charge and which instructions are current.
cards.summary: Coordination services are small, strongly consistent (consensus-replicated) key-value stores for coordination, not bulk data. They provide leader election, distributed locks and leases, service discovery, configuration, and cluster membership through watches and ephemeral keys. etcd stores all Kubernetes state. ZooKeeper historically coordinated Kafka, HBase and Hadoop; Kafka has replaced it with its own KRaft quorum.

sections.title: Use it well
items: Keep data tiny (KBs to MBs), and keep writes infrequent.
A lock needs a fencing token (a monotonic number checked by the resource). Otherwise a paused client can act on an expired lease.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Losing quorum (for example 2 of 3 nodes) blocks all writes and leader changes. Run 3 or 5 nodes across zones.
Abusing it as a general database causes slow disks, huge snapshots and election storms.

cards.title: Google Cloud Storage Buckets
cards.subtitle: GCS · gs:// · the data lake and model store on GCP
cards.lego: Google's version of the giant storage bins, with a choice of how close to the front door each bin sits (and what it costs to open).
cards.summary: GCS is Google Cloud's object store. Objects live in buckets under a flat namespace with '/' only as a naming convention. Location types are region, dual-region and multi-region. Storage classes are Standard, Nearline (30-day minimum), Coldline (90-day) and Archive (365-day), with Autoclass available to tier automatically. It offers strong global consistency for object reads, writes and listing, IAM with uniform bucket-level access, signed URLs, object versioning, lifecycle rules, and Pub/Sub notifications. It is the default landing zone for data lakes, Spark and Dataproc jobs, BigQuery external tables, training data and model artifacts.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Raw and curated data-lake zones (Parquet or Iceberg files), batch pipeline inputs and outputs.
ML datasets, checkpoints and model weights. Mount with Cloud Storage FUSE, or stream with parallel readers.
Media and static assets behind Cloud CDN. Backups and logs with lifecycle rules to cheaper classes.

sections.title: Design tips
items: Co-locate buckets with compute (same region) to avoid egress cost and latency.
Ramp request rates gradually. Very high QPS on sequential names (timestamps) can hot-spot, so prefer random or hashed prefixes.
Use Pub/Sub notifications or Eventarc to trigger pipelines when objects land. Delivery is at-least-once, so make consumers idempotent.
Many small files hurt Spark and BigQuery. Compact them into files of about 128 MB to 1 GB.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Early deletion fees and retrieval costs on cold classes surprise batch jobs that reread old data.
A publicly readable bucket through a mistaken IAM binding. Enforce public access prevention.
Loading model weights from GCS on every pod start slows GPU autoscaling. Cache or pre-stage the weights.

cards.title: DNS & Global Traffic Routing
cards.subtitle: Amazon Route 53 · Cloudflare DNS · Google Cloud DNS
cards.lego: The address printed on the box lid. Before anyone can touch your model, they have to find which table it's sitting on.
cards.summary: DNS turns names into IP addresses through a hierarchy of cached lookups, and each record has a TTL. Managed DNS can also route: by latency or geography to the nearest region, by weight for canaries and blue/green deploys, and by failover when health checks fail.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: This is always the first hop: every request starts with a lookup.
Multi-region active-active or active-passive failover.
Weighted shifts of traffic between old and new stacks.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Caching makes changes slow to propagate. They take at least the TTL to spread, and some clients ignore TTLs.
Short TTLs mean faster failover but more lookups and more dependence on the DNS provider.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: An outage at the DNS provider makes healthy services unreachable, as in the 2016 Dyn attack.
A long TTL on a record pointing at a dead region keeps sending users there.

cards.title: Load Balancers
cards.subtitle: AWS ALB/NLB · NGINX · HAProxy · Envoy
cards.lego: The traffic manager that splits an incoming stream of LEGO pegs evenly across many identical worker bricks, and stops feeding any brick that has cracked.
cards.summary: A load balancer spreads requests across a pool of healthy targets. Layer 4 balancers route raw TCP or UDP connections and are fast and simple. Layer 7 balancers understand HTTP: they route by path or header, terminate TLS, and retry. Common algorithms are round-robin, least-connections and consistent hashing (for stickiness). Health checks eject failing targets.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: You scale any stateless tier horizontally, whether web servers, APIs or workers behind RPC.
You want TLS termination in one place, zero-downtime deploys, and blue/green or canary releases.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: The balancer itself must be highly available: use a managed service, or a redundant pair with a floating IP or anycast.
Sticky sessions undermine even distribution and make scaling in painful. Prefer stateless servers.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: A health check that is too shallow keeps a server in rotation that returns 200 while its database is gone.
A health check that is too deep (it checks the database) means one database blip ejects every target and causes a total outage.
Long-lived connections (WebSockets, gRPC) stay pinned to old servers, so newly added servers get no load.

cards.title: API Gateway
cards.subtitle: Amazon API Gateway · Kong · Apigee · Envoy Gateway
cards.lego: The single front-door stud every piece must pass through. It checks your ticket, limits how fast you can push, and routes you to the right sub-assembly.
cards.summary: A single entry point in front of many backend services. It handles cross-cutting concerns in one place: authentication and authorization, rate limits and quotas, routing by path or version, request and response transformation, protocol translation (REST to gRPC), and metrics and tracing. A Backend-for-Frontend (BFF) is a gateway tailored to one client, such as mobile.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Mobile and web clients talk to many microservices, and you don't want each client to know about each service.
You expose public APIs that need keys, quotas and usage plans.
You want auth, throttling and observability configured once rather than in every service.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: It adds a network hop and a component that must scale and stay highly available.
Business logic tends to creep in. Keep the gateway thin.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: One bad routing or auth config change takes every API down at once. Roll out config gradually.
Without per-client limits, one noisy client starves everyone else.

cards.title: Content Delivery Network
cards.subtitle: Amazon CloudFront · Cloudflare · Akamai · Fastly
cards.lego: Small caching outposts built on every block of the city, so kids grab pieces from the corner shop instead of walking to the main warehouse.
cards.summary: A CDN is a global network of edge servers (points of presence, or PoPs) that cache content close to users. It cuts latency and offloads your origin. It serves static assets, video segments and downloads, can cache some dynamic responses, terminates TLS near the user, and absorbs DDoS attacks. Edge compute such as Workers or Lambda@Edge runs logic there.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Images, JS/CSS, fonts, video (HLS/DASH segments), software downloads.
You have a global audience, or you need DDoS protection and a web application firewall at the edge.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Invalidation is hard. Prefer versioned, content-hashed filenames (app.3f9a.js) with long TTLs.
Personalized or rapidly changing responses cache poorly.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: A global purge or a cold cache sends every miss to the origin at once. Add an origin shield or tiered cache.
Caching private responses (a missing Cache-Control: private) leaks one user's data to another.
Stale assets after a deploy break the page if HTML and JS versions mismatch.

cards.title: Service Mesh: Istio
cards.subtitle: Istio · Envoy · Linkerd · ambient mode
cards.lego: A clip-on connector attached to every brick, so every connection between bricks is locked, counted and steerable without redesigning the bricks themselves.
cards.summary: A service mesh moves service-to-service networking out of application code into a proxy layer. In sidecar mode an Envoy proxy runs next to every pod; in ambient mode per-node ztunnel proxies handle L4 and optional waypoint proxies handle L7. The control plane (istiod) pushes configuration to the proxies. You get mutual TLS and workload identity, fine-grained traffic management (weighted canaries, header routing, retries, timeouts, circuit breaking, fault injection, mirroring), authorization policy, and uniform metrics and traces.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Many microservices on Kubernetes need zero-trust mTLS and consistent retries, timeouts and telemetry.
Progressive delivery: shift 1% → 10% → 100% of traffic to a new version, or mirror production traffic to a shadow model.
Chaos drills: inject delays and aborts with a VirtualService, no code changes needed.

sections.title: Key resources
items: Gateway (ingress and egress), VirtualService (routing rules), DestinationRule (subsets, load balancing, outlier detection), PeerAuthentication and AuthorizationPolicy (mTLS and access).

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Sidecars add memory and CPU per pod and extra latency per hop, which ambient mode reduces.
Mesh-level retries stacked on client retries multiply load. Own retries in one layer.
A bad mesh config push can break traffic cluster-wide. Canary your control-plane changes.

cards.title: Torbit: Walmart's Edge Platform
cards.subtitle: Edge proxy · L7 routing · edge caching and security
cards.lego: Walmart's own front gate and sorting station at the edge of the city. Every visitor passes through it before reaching any building, and it decides which building they go to.
cards.summary: Torbit began as a web-performance startup (real-user monitoring and dynamic front-end optimization) that Walmart Labs acquired in 2013. The team went on to build Walmart's in-house edge infrastructure: proxies, load balancers, edge security and real-user monitoring. Walmart engineers use Torbit for edge traffic control such as path-based routing between legacy and new services. Conceptually it plays the role of a CDN or edge proxy plus L7 load balancer in front of the origin: TLS termination, caching, request routing and rewriting, bot and WAF protection, and gradual traffic shifting.

sections.title: Where it sits
items: Client → DNS → Torbit edge (TLS, cache, security, routing) → regional load balancers or ingress (Istio gateway) → services.
The public equivalent is Cloudflare, Akamai or Fastly, combined with an Envoy or NGINX edge tier.

sections.title: Use it for
items: Path-based migration: route /api/cart/* to the new microservice at 10%, then increase, with instant rollback at the edge.
Shielding origins from flash-sale spikes with caching, rate limits and request collapsing.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: An edge misconfiguration affects everything behind it. Stage and canary routing changes.
Caching personalized responses leaks data. Split what is cacheable from what is personalized.

cards.title: Message Queues
cards.subtitle: Amazon SQS · RabbitMQ · Google Cloud Tasks
cards.lego: A buffer tray between two builders. When one passes pieces faster than the next can snap them in, the pieces wait safely in the tray instead of falling on the floor.
cards.summary: Producers put messages on a durable queue and consumers pull them, process them, and then acknowledge (delete) them. Each message goes to one consumer (point-to-point). The queue decouples the producer from the consumer's speed and availability, levels out bursts, and makes retries easy. Most queues deliver at least once, so a message can arrive more than once.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Background jobs: emails, video encoding, report generation, order fulfilment.
Load leveling: absorb a 10× spike and drain it at the rate the database can handle.
Spreading work across a pool of workers that you scale on queue depth.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Processing becomes asynchronous: the user sees 'processing…' and the result arrives later.
Ordering is not guaranteed unless you use FIFO queues or message groups, which limit throughput.
At-least-once delivery means duplicates, so handlers must be idempotent.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: A poison message fails forever and blocks or wastes workers. Move it to a dead-letter queue (DLQ) after N attempts.
If the visibility timeout is shorter than processing time, the message reappears and is processed twice.
If consumers are permanently slower than producers, the backlog grows without bound. Queues absorb bursts; they don't fix sustained overload.

cards.title: Event Streams
cards.subtitle: Apache Kafka · Amazon Kinesis · Redpanda · Google Pub/Sub
cards.lego: A central conveyor belt that constantly carries every change past every station. Each station takes what it needs, and the belt remembers what went by so a station can rewind.
cards.summary: A stream is an append-only log, split into partitions and replicated across brokers. Consumers track their own offsets, so many independent consumer groups can read the same events at their own pace. Retention lets you replay history. Order is guaranteed within a partition, and all events with the same key land in the same partition.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Fan-out: one event (OrderPlaced, DriverMoved) feeds many services such as billing, analytics, search and notifications.
Change data capture from a database, real-time analytics, activity and telemetry pipelines.
Event sourcing, or rebuilding a read model by replaying history.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Clusters, partitions and schemas are heavy to operate.
Order holds only within a partition, and consumer parallelism is capped at the partition count.
Exactly-once processing needs idempotent producers plus transactions or idempotent sinks.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Consumer lag grows until data ages out of retention before a slow consumer reads it.
A skewed key (one busy city, one mega-customer) creates a hot partition.
Rebalancing storms pause every consumer in the group while partitions are reassigned.

sections.title: Queue vs stream
items: Queue: a message is consumed once, then deleted. Good for work distribution.
Stream: an event is retained, read by many, and can be replayed. Good for broadcasting facts.

cards.title: Caches
cards.subtitle: Redis · Memcached · Valkey · in-process caches
cards.lego: An ultra-fast shelf at arm's reach for the pieces you grab most, so you don't open the heavy bottom drawer (the database) every time.
cards.summary: A cache is an in-memory key-value store that answers in under a millisecond. The common patterns are cache-aside (the app reads the cache, and on a miss loads from the database and fills the cache), read-through, write-through and write-behind. Entries expire by TTL and are evicted by LRU or LFU. Redis adds data structures such as sorted sets for leaderboards, geo indexes, counters, streams and pub/sub.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Reads far outnumber writes and the same hot data is read over and over.
Sessions, rate-limit counters, leaderboards, feature flags, computed or aggregated results.
Fast geo lookups, such as nearby drivers, with Redis GEO.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Staleness: you choose how wrong the data is allowed to be, and for how long.
Invalidation adds complexity, and memory costs more than disk.
It is another system that can fail or disagree with the source of truth.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Stampede (thundering herd): a hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at once. Fix with request coalescing, locks or leases, or early refresh.
A cold cache after a restart or failover sends the full read load to the database.
Treating the cache as the source of truth loses data on eviction or restart.

sections.title: Remember
items: Main memory ≈ 100 ns, SSD read ≈ 100 µs, a same-datacenter round trip ≈ 0.5 ms.
Track the hit ratio. Going from a 90% to a 99% hit rate cuts database load 10×.

cards.title: Apache Kafka Deep Dive
cards.subtitle: Brokers · topics · partitions · consumer groups · KRaft
cards.lego: The master conveyor belt, split into parallel lanes (partitions). Each lane keeps its pieces in order, and every station bookmarks how far down each lane it has read.
cards.summary: A topic is split into partitions. Each partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on a leader broker and replicated to followers; the in-sync replica set is the ISR. Producers choose the partition by key hash, and batch and compress records. Consumers in a group split the partitions between them (one partition to at most one consumer in the group) and commit offsets. Retention is by time or size, or by compaction to the latest value per key. KRaft (a Raft metadata quorum) has replaced ZooKeeper. Kafka Connect moves data in and out; Kafka Streams and Flink process it.

sections.title: Durability knobs
items: Producer acks=all, enable.idempotence=true, and topic min.insync.replicas=2 with replication factor 3 means no loss if one broker dies.
Transactions plus read_committed consumers give exactly-once read-process-write within Kafka.

sections.title: Sizing and scaling
items: Partitions cap consumer parallelism. Choose for peak throughput per consumer, with headroom, because adding partitions later reshuffles key-to-partition mapping.
Key by the entity whose events must stay ordered (order_id, driver_id), and watch for skew.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Consumer rebalances: a slow handler exceeds max.poll.interval.ms, the consumer is kicked out, partitions move, lag spikes. Decouple polling from processing.
Under-replicated partitions and unclean leader election lead to data loss. Keep unclean.leader.election.enable=false.
Poison messages block a partition. Route them to a dead-letter topic after N retries.

sections.title: At Walmart
items: Walmart describes 25,000+ Kafka consumers processing trillions of messages a day. Its Messaging Proxy Service decouples consumption from processing to avoid rebalance-driven lag.

cards.title: Distributed Cache
cards.subtitle: Redis Cluster · Memcached pools · Netflix EVCache · client-side sharding
cards.lego: Many arm's-reach shelves spread down a long table, with a rule that tells every builder which shelf a given piece lives on, and spare shelves that hold copies.
cards.summary: When one cache node isn't enough memory or throughput, keys are partitioned across many nodes. Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots assigned to primaries with replicas; Memcached uses client-side consistent hashing, often through a proxy such as mcrouter or twemproxy. Replicas and zone-aware copies add availability, and cross-region replication (for example through Kafka, as in Netflix EVCache) keeps global caches warm. A near cache (in-process L1) in front of the distributed L2 absorbs the hottest keys.

sections.title: Design choices
items: Sharding: Redis Cluster hash slots or consistent hashing, so adding a node moves only about 1/N of keys.
Replication: a replica per shard for failover, and copies in each zone so reads stay local.
Consistency: invalidate on write (preferably driven by change data capture), TTL as a safety net, versioned keys for immutable data.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Hot keys: one shard melts while the rest idle. Replicate hot keys, add an L1 near cache, or split the key.
Node loss or resharding means a cold slice and a database spike. Warm the cache gradually and coalesce requests.
Big values or keys (multi-MB) cause latency spikes and network saturation.
Multi-key operations fail across slots in Redis Cluster. Use hash tags {user42}:… to co-locate keys.

cards.title: Metrics & Alerting: Prometheus
cards.subtitle: Prometheus · Grafana · Alertmanager · Thanos / Mimir
cards.lego: Gauges clipped onto every brick, read every few seconds and written into a logbook, with an alarm bell when a needle crosses the red line.
cards.summary: Prometheus pulls (scrapes) metrics over HTTP from /metrics endpoints every 15–60 s and stores them as time series identified by a metric name and labels, in a compressed time-series database. The metric types are counters, gauges, histograms and summaries. You query with PromQL, for example rate(http_requests_total[5m]) and histogram_quantile(0.99, …). Alertmanager deduplicates and routes alerts. Grafana draws dashboards. Thanos, Cortex or Mimir add long-term, global, highly available storage.

sections.title: What to measure
items: RED for services: request Rate, Errors, Duration (as histograms, for p50/p95/p99).
USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors (CPU, memory, disk, GPU, queue depth).
The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Alert on SLO burn rate, not on raw CPU.

sections.title: For LLM serving
items: Time to first token (TTFT), time per output token (TPOT), tokens per second, running and waiting requests, KV-cache usage, GPU utilization (DCGM exporter). vLLM, SGLang and Triton expose Prometheus metrics.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Cardinality explosion: putting user_id or request_id in labels creates millions of series and exhausts memory.
Averages hide tails. Averaging precomputed quantiles across instances is mathematically wrong; aggregate histograms instead.

cards.title: Distributed Tracing & Logs
cards.subtitle: OpenTelemetry · Jaeger · Tempo · structured logging
cards.lego: A tracer dye on one peg, so you can watch exactly which bricks it passed through and how long it paused at each.
cards.summary: A trace follows one request across services as a tree of spans (with service, operation, duration and attributes), linked by a trace ID propagated in headers (W3C traceparent). OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard: SDKs plus a Collector for traces, metrics and logs. Sampling (head-based or tail-based) keeps costs sane. Structured JSON logs that carry the trace ID tie the three signals together.

sections.title: Use it for
items: Finding which hop inflated the p99, spotting fan-out N+1 calls, and tracing a request through gateway, mesh, model server and database.

sections.title: Watch out
items: Missing context propagation (async queues, thread pools) breaks traces. Pass the context through Kafka headers.
Log volume costs: sample debug logs and never log prompts or PII by default.

links.title: Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure

cards.title: Vertical vs Horizontal Scaling
cards.subtitle: Scale up vs scale out
cards.lego: Swap a small brick for a giant brick (vertical), or add more identical bricks side by side (horizontal).
cards.summary: Vertical scaling gives one machine more CPU, RAM or disk. It is simple, needs no code changes, and hits a ceiling and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds more machines behind a load balancer or partitioning scheme. It has almost no ceiling and survives a node failure, but requires stateless services or partitioned data.

sections.title: Rules of thumb
items: Scale the stateless tiers horizontally first; it's cheap and easy.
Scale databases vertically as far as is sensible, then add read replicas, then shard.
Autoscale on a leading signal (queue depth, concurrency) rather than a lagging one (CPU at 90%).

sections.title: Watch out
items: Horizontal scale moves the bottleneck downstream. Fifty more app servers can open 5,000 more database connections.

links.title: Designs, Lessons and Advice from Building Large Distributed Systems

cards.title: Stateless Services
cards.subtitle: Share-nothing application tiers
cards.lego: Every worker brick is identical and remembers nothing, so any brick can be swapped, added or thrown away without the model noticing.
cards.summary: A stateless server keeps no user data between requests in its own memory or disk. Sessions, uploads and job state live in shared stores: a database, a cache, object storage or a signed token (such as a JWT). Then the load balancer can send any request to any instance, and instances can be killed or added freely.

sections.title: Why it matters
items: Enables autoscaling, rolling deploys, spot instances and serverless.
Removes the need for sticky sessions, and failover just works.

sections.title: Where the state goes
items: Session data goes to Redis or a signed cookie or JWT.
Uploaded files go to object storage. Work in progress goes to a queue or database.

cards.title: Replication
cards.subtitle: Leader-follower · multi-leader · leaderless quorums
cards.lego: Build identical copies of the same model on different tables, so if one table collapses, the others still stand.
cards.summary: Replication keeps copies of the same data on several nodes, for availability, read scaling and locality. In leader-follower replication, one node takes writes and followers replay its log (Postgres, MySQL). In multi-leader replication, several regions accept writes and must resolve conflicts. Leaderless systems (Dynamo, Cassandra) write to W of N replicas and read from R of N; when R + W > N, a read overlaps the latest write.

sections.title: Key choices
items: Synchronous replication means no data loss on failover but slower writes. Asynchronous means fast writes but possible loss and lag.
Automatic failover needs consensus (Raft, Paxos) or a coordinator to avoid split-brain, where two nodes both think they are leader.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Replication lag: a user writes, then reads from a follower and doesn't see the change. Fix with read-your-writes routing.
An asynchronous leader dies before shipping its last writes, and they are lost after failover.

cards.title: Sharding (Partitioning)
cards.subtitle: Split one dataset across many databases
cards.lego: The model is too big for one table, so you split it into sections and give each table one section, using a rule everyone agrees on to know which section lives where.
cards.summary: Sharding splits data by a shard key so each node holds a subset. Range sharding (by date or by A–M) makes range scans easy but creates hot spots. Hash sharding spreads load evenly but loses range locality. Directory or lookup sharding maps keys to shards in a table, which is flexible but adds a lookup. Choose the key so most queries hit exactly one shard.

sections.title: Choosing a shard key
items: Use what nearly every query filters by: tenant_id, user_id, channel_id.
It needs high cardinality and evenly spread traffic. Avoid time or other monotonically increasing keys for hash-less range shards.

sections.title: Costs
items: Cross-shard joins and transactions become application problems.
Resharding is painful. Use many logical shards mapped onto fewer physical nodes so you can move them later.
Celebrity keys still create hot shards and need special handling.

cards.title: Consistent Hashing
cards.subtitle: Stable key placement as nodes come and go
cards.lego: Arrange the tables in a circle. Each piece goes to the next table clockwise, so adding a table only takes pieces from its one neighbour.
cards.summary: Nodes and keys are hashed onto the same ring, and each key belongs to the first node clockwise from it. Adding or removing a node moves only about 1/N of the keys, compared with nearly all of them under hash(key) mod N. Virtual nodes (many points per server) smooth out the load. It is used by Dynamo, Cassandra, CDNs, cache clusters and load balancers (Maglev).

sections.title: Remember
items: Plain modulo hashing reshuffles almost every key when N changes, which is a cache-miss storm.
Replicate by storing each key on the next R distinct nodes around the ring.

cards.title: CAP & PACELC
cards.subtitle: What you give up when the network splits, and when it doesn't
cards.lego: Two halves of the model are separated by a gap. Either both halves stop changing until they can talk again (consistency), or each keeps building on its own and you reconcile later (availability).
cards.summary: CAP says that during a network partition (P), a system must choose between consistency (C: every read sees the latest write, or gets an error) and availability (A: every request gets an answer, possibly stale). PACELC adds that Else, when there is no partition, you still trade latency (L) against consistency (C). For example, DynamoDB's default eventual reads favour latency, while Spanner favours consistency.

sections.title: Use it well
items: Partitions aren't optional, so the real question is how each operation behaves when one happens.
Choose per operation, not per system: bank balances need C, like counts can take A.
Most real systems are neither pure CP nor pure AP. Describe the exact consistency guarantee instead.

cards.title: Consistency Models
cards.subtitle: Linearizable · read-your-writes · monotonic · eventual
cards.lego: How quickly does everyone around the table see the brick you just placed: instantly, only you, or eventually?
cards.summary: Consistency models range from strong to weak. Linearizable means the system behaves like a single copy, and every read sees the latest completed write. Sequential and causal consistency preserve order and cause-and-effect. Read-your-writes guarantees you always see your own updates. Monotonic reads guarantee you never go back in time. Eventual consistency only promises that replicas converge when writes stop.

sections.title: Pick per feature
items: Payments, inventory, unique usernames and leader election need linearizable operations.
A profile edit needs read-your-writes: route that user's reads to the leader for a few seconds.
Feeds, like counts and analytics can be eventual.

cards.title: Caching Patterns & Invalidation
cards.subtitle: Cache-aside · write-through · write-behind · TTLs
cards.lego: Decide when the arm's-reach shelf is refilled, and when a piece on it is too old to trust.
cards.summary: Cache-aside (lazy loading) is the default: read the cache, on a miss read the database, then set the cache with a TTL. Write-through updates the cache and the database together. Write-behind writes the cache first and flushes to the database asynchronously, which is fast but can lose data. For invalidation, prefer deleting the key on write over updating it, always set a TTL as a safety net, and use versioned keys for immutable data.

sections.title: Stampede defences
items: Request coalescing (single-flight): one request fetches while the others wait for its result.
Leases or locks per key, as in Facebook's memcache.
Refresh popular keys before they expire, and add jitter to TTLs so keys don't expire together.

sections.title: Gotchas
items: A race between 'delete on write' and a concurrent cache fill can store stale data. Leases or short TTLs contain it.
Negative caching (remembering 'not found') prevents repeated misses for missing keys.

cards.title: Sagas & the Transactional Outbox
cards.subtitle: Consistency across services without distributed locks
cards.lego: A multi-builder assembly where each builder finishes their part and passes a note to the next. If a later step fails, each builder takes back their own part in reverse order.
cards.summary: Once data is spread across services, one ACID transaction can't cover it, and two-phase commit is fragile. A saga is a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action (for example, refund the payment and release the stock). The transactional outbox fixes the dual-write problem: write the business row and an 'event to publish' row in the same local transaction, and a relay publishes the outbox rows to the queue or stream.

sections.title: Why the outbox
items: 'Update the database, then publish to Kafka' can crash in between, and you get an order with no event.
The outbox plus at-least-once relay plus idempotent consumers gives an effectively-once outcome.

sections.title: Orchestration vs choreography
items: Orchestration: a central coordinator tells each service what to do. Easier to follow and monitor.
Choreography: services react to each other's events. Looser coupling, but harder to see the whole flow.

cards.title: Unique ID Generation
cards.subtitle: Auto-increment · UUID · Snowflake IDs
cards.lego: Every brick needs a serial number stamped on it, and thousands of factories must stamp numbers at the same time without ever printing the same one twice.
cards.summary: A single database auto-increment is simple but becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure. UUIDv4 is random, needs no coordination, and fragments B-tree indexes. Snowflake-style IDs pack a timestamp, a machine ID and a per-millisecond sequence into 64 bits, so they are unique, roughly time-sortable and generated locally. UUIDv7 is a time-ordered UUID standard.

sections.title: Use it for
items: URL shortener keys (encode the number in base62), tweet and post IDs, order numbers, shard-aware IDs (put the shard ID inside the ID).

sections.title: Watch out
items: If a clock moves backwards, a Snowflake generator can issue duplicates. Refuse to issue IDs until the clock catches up.
Sequential public IDs leak business volume and invite scraping.

cards.title: Idempotency
cards.subtitle: Idempotency keys make retries safe
cards.lego: Pressing the same brick onto the same stud twice leaves one brick, not two.
cards.summary: An operation is idempotent if doing it several times has the same effect as doing it once. The client sends a unique Idempotency-Key with each logical request (for example, one checkout attempt). The server stores the key with the result, and a retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging again. This is what makes at-least-once delivery and automatic retries safe.

sections.title: Implementation
items: Enforce uniqueness on (client, key) in the database. Insert the key first; if the insert conflicts, return the saved response.
Keep keys for longer than the longest retry window, for example 24 hours.
Natural idempotency: PUT and DELETE, 'set status = shipped', upserts keyed by event ID.

cards.title: Timeouts, Retries, Backoff & Jitter
cards.subtitle: Fail fast, retry politely
cards.lego: If a builder doesn't answer, wait a bit before asking again, wait longer each time, and don't let the whole room shout at the same moment.
cards.summary: Every network call needs a timeout; without one, a slow dependency ties up your threads forever. Retry only transient errors, and only idempotent operations. Space retries out with exponential backoff (for example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms…) plus random jitter so clients don't retry in sync. Cap the number of attempts, and use a retry budget so retries can't multiply load during an outage.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Retry storms: three layers each retrying three times turns one failure into 27 calls.
Retries without jitter synchronize into waves that knock the dependency down again.

cards.title: Circuit Breakers & Bulkheads
cards.subtitle: Contain failures before they cascade
cards.lego: A breaker switch between sub-assemblies that snaps open when one keeps failing, plus walls between sections so a collapse in one doesn't topple the rest.
cards.summary: A circuit breaker counts failures to a dependency. Past a threshold it opens and fails fast, often returning a fallback. After a cooldown it half-opens and lets a few trial calls through, closing again if they succeed. Bulkheads give each dependency its own thread pool or connection pool, so one slow dependency can't take every thread.

sections.title: Fallbacks
items: Serve cached or default data, hide the feature (no recommendations row), or queue the request for later.
A fallback must be cheaper and more reliable than the thing it replaces.

cards.title: Rate Limiting
cards.subtitle: Token bucket · leaky bucket · fixed and sliding windows
cards.lego: A turnstile on the front-door stud: each visitor gets a handful of tokens that refill slowly, and no tokens means no entry.
cards.summary: A rate limiter caps how many requests a client (by user, API key or IP) can make. A token bucket allows bursts up to the bucket size and a sustained refill rate. A sliding window gives smoother limits than fixed windows, which allow double bursts at window edges. In a distributed system, keep counters in Redis and update them atomically (INCR with EXPIRE, or a Lua script). Reject with HTTP 429 and a Retry-After header.

sections.title: Design choices
items: Where: at the gateway, per service, or both.
Fail open or fail closed when the limiter's store is down.
Layer the limits: per-user limits, global load shedding, and reserved capacity for critical traffic.

cards.title: Backpressure & Load Shedding
cards.subtitle: Say 'slow down' or 'no' before you fall over
cards.lego: When the builder's hands are full, they stop accepting pieces, or politely drop the least important ones, instead of letting everything crash to the floor.
cards.summary: Backpressure pushes the signal to slow down back upstream: bounded queues, blocking producers, HTTP 429 or 503. Load shedding deliberately rejects excess or low-priority work so the rest finishes in time. A server at 110% capacity that accepts everything often completes nothing, because every request times out after doing its work.

sections.title: Techniques
items: Bounded queues and concurrency limits, which can adapt to measured latency.
Prioritize: checkout over recommendations, interactive over batch.
Drop requests whose client deadline has already passed.

cards.title: Delivery Semantics
cards.subtitle: At-most-once · at-least-once · exactly-once
cards.lego: Will each piece on the conveyor arrive zero or one time, one or more times, or exactly once?
cards.summary: At-most-once means acknowledging before processing: messages can be lost but never duplicated. At-least-once means acknowledging after processing: nothing is lost but duplicates happen, and it is the default for SQS, Kafka consumers and S3 events. Exactly-once delivery isn't possible over an unreliable network in general, but exactly-once effects are: combine at-least-once delivery with idempotent processing or transactional sinks (Kafka transactions, dedupe tables).

sections.title: Remember
items: Design for at-least-once plus idempotency. It's the pragmatic answer in nearly every interview and production system.

cards.title: Latency Numbers & Tail Latency
cards.subtitle: Know the orders of magnitude
cards.lego: Know how far each drawer is from your hands before you decide where to keep a piece.
cards.summary: Rough orders of magnitude: L1 cache ≈ 1 ns, main memory ≈ 100 ns, SSD random read ≈ 100 µs, a round trip in the same datacenter ≈ 0.5 ms, a disk seek ≈ 10 ms, and a round trip across a continent ≈ 50–150 ms. Tail latency (p99, p999) dominates at scale. If a page fans out to 100 backends, a 1-in-100 slow response slows most page loads.

sections.title: Tail tolerance
items: Hedged requests: after the p95 time, send a second copy of the request and use whichever answers first.
Measure percentiles, not averages. Set timeouts from the p99.
