cards.title: Back-of-the-Envelope Estimation
cards.subtitle: Size it before you draw it
cards.lego: Count how many pieces you need before you pick the baseplate.
cards.summary: Estimate the load for a photo-sharing app with 100 million daily active users, where each user views 50 photos and uploads 0.5 photos per day, and an average photo is 500 KB. Work out the read QPS, write QPS, peak QPS, daily new storage and 5-year storage.
steps: Seconds per day ≈ 86,400 ≈ 10^5. So 1 million requests a day ≈ 12 per second.
Reads: 100M × 50 = 5 billion per day, so about 58,000 QPS on average.
Writes: 100M × 0.5 = 50 million per day, so about 580 QPS. The read-to-write ratio is 100:1, which says read-heavy: cache and CDN.
Peak ≈ 2–3× average, so plan for about 150,000 read QPS and 1,500 write QPS.
Storage: 50M × 500 KB = 25 TB per day, about 9 PB per year, about 45 PB over 5 years before replication. That means object storage with lifecycle tiers.
Metadata: 50M rows per day × about 1 KB = 50 GB per day, which fits a sharded database or a NoSQL table.

sections.title: Handy constants
items: 2^10 ≈ a thousand, 2^20 ≈ a million, 2^30 ≈ a billion, 2^40 ≈ a trillion (KB, MB, GB, TB).
One modern server handles very roughly 10k–100k simple requests per second. One Postgres primary, very roughly 10k–50k simple writes per second.
Round aggressively. The goal is the order of magnitude, not the decimal.

links.title: Latency Numbers Every Programmer Should Know

cards.title: Availability, SLOs & Error Budgets
cards.subtitle: How many nines, and what they cost
cards.lego: Decide how often the model is allowed to have a missing brick, and spend that allowance on shipping new features.
cards.summary: An SLI is a measured indicator, such as the share of requests that succeed in under 300 ms. An SLO is the target for it, such as 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is a contract with penalties. The error budget is 1 minus the SLO; while budget remains you ship faster, and when it runs out you focus on reliability. Components in series multiply their availabilities (99.9% × 99.9% ≈ 99.8%); redundant components in parallel raise it.

sections.title: The nines
items: 99% ≈ 3.65 days of downtime a year (7.3 hours a month).
99.9% ≈ 8.8 hours a year (43.8 minutes a month).
99.99% ≈ 52.6 minutes a year (4.4 minutes a month).
99.999% ≈ 5.3 minutes a year. Each extra nine costs roughly 10× more.

cards.title: Uber-like Ride-Hailing
cards.subtitle: Example A · real-time geospatial matching
cards.lego: A city-sized model where hundreds of thousands of tiny car bricks keep moving, and every few seconds a passenger brick asks, 'which car is closest to me?'
cards.summary: Hundreds of thousands of drivers broadcast their location every few seconds. Passengers request rides and must be matched to a nearby available driver in real time, without two passengers getting the same driver.
steps: An API Gateway authenticates the driver apps and receives a location ping (driver_id, lat, lng, status) every ~4 seconds.
Pings go straight onto an event stream (Kafka), keyed by geo cell (for example an H3 index) so each region's updates stay ordered. The gateway never writes to a database per ping.

A geospatial compute cluster (containers) consumes the stream and updates an in-memory cache (Redis GEO, or H3 cell → driver sets) with each driver's latest position and a short TTL, so drivers who go silent disappear on their own. Other consumers, such as ETA, surge pricing and analytics, read the same stream independently.

When a passenger requests a ride, a serverless function (or matching service) asks Redis for available drivers within a radius, ranks them by ETA, and claims one atomically (for example SET driver:lock NX with a TTL) to prevent double dispatch.

The match goes into a message queue, and a notifier sends the driver a push notification with retries and a timeout. If the driver declines or doesn't answer, the lock is released and the next candidate is offered.
The confirmed trip is written to a durable database (sharded by city or trip ID) as the system of record for billing and history.

sections.title: Why these bricks
items: Location is high-volume and short-lived. Keep only the latest position in memory; the stream holds history for replay and analytics.
The stream decouples ingestion from consumers, so a slow analytics job never delays matching.
Geo cells turn 'nearby' into a handful of key lookups instead of scanning every driver.
The queue makes notifications reliable and retryable without blocking the matcher.

sections.title: Numbers
items: 500,000 active drivers × 1 ping every 4 s ≈ 125,000 writes per second of ingest.
Each position ≈ 100 bytes, so all active drivers fit in well under 1 GB of RAM.

sections.title: Break it
items: A Redis shard dies: its drivers vanish until their next ping (about 4 s) or until the cache is rebuilt from the stream. Is a few seconds of blindness acceptable?
Friday night downtown: one geo cell's partition runs hot. Split cells into finer resolution or sub-partitions.
Two matchers pick the same driver: without the atomic claim, both riders get a confirmation.
The push provider slows down: the queue backlog grows, so set a message TTL and re-match instead of sending stale offers.

links.title: H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index

cards.title: E-commerce Flash-Sale Checkout
cards.subtitle: Example B · surviving a purchase surge
cards.lego: Doors open on a toy-store sale. Instead of everyone rushing the one cash register (the database), customers drop numbered tickets in a slot, and a clerk processes them one by one.
cards.summary: During a flash sale, millions of shoppers try to buy at the same moment. Handle the surge without dropping orders, overselling limited stock, or charging anyone twice.
steps: A CDN serves the product pages and static assets, and an API Gateway applies per-user rate limits (optionally a virtual waiting room) so the origin sees only real checkout attempts.
Load balancers spread millions of concurrent requests across hundreds of stateless checkout containers that autoscale.
Each checkout reserves stock atomically in a fast store (a Redis DECR, or a conditional UPDATE … WHERE stock > 0) and rejects immediately when stock is gone.
Instead of writing the full order to the database under peak load, the container drops an order message (with a client-generated idempotency key) onto a durable message queue.
The user instantly sees 'Your order is processing', and the page polls or receives a push when the order is confirmed.

Isolated order-processing workers pull jobs at a steady pace the database can handle. Each worker writes the order to the relational database in a transaction, calls the payment gateway with the same idempotency key, and acknowledges the message only after both succeed.
Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue for inspection. An outbox table publishes OrderConfirmed events for email, fulfilment and analytics.

sections.title: Why these bricks
items: The queue turns a spike the database can't survive into a steady flow it can (load leveling).
Stateless containers scale out instantly; the database doesn't, so it is protected behind the queue.
Idempotency keys make every retry safe, whether from the browser, the queue or the payment call.

sections.title: Numbers
items: 1 million orders in 10 minutes ≈ 1,700 orders per second on average, with the first seconds at 10× that. Workers might drain 2,000 per second.

sections.title: Break it
items: A worker crashes after charging but before acknowledging: the message reappears, and the idempotency key stops a second charge.
The payment gateway times out: retry with backoff and the same key. Never generate a new key on retry.
The queue backlog grows: autoscale workers on queue depth, but cap them at the database's safe concurrency and show an honest ETA.
The Redis stock count and the database disagree after a crash: reconcile, and choose reserve-then-confirm with expiring reservations.

links.title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency
Surviving Flashes of High-Write Traffic Using Scriptable Load Balancers
A Pods Architecture To Allow Shopify To Scale

cards.title: URL Shortener at Scale
cards.subtitle: Like bit.ly or TinyURL
cards.lego: A giant wall of tiny labelled drawers: each short label opens a drawer holding the long address.
cards.summary: Design a service that turns long URLs into 7-character short links and redirects about 100 million clicks a day with low latency. Reads outnumber writes about 100 to 1.
steps: Write path: POST /links {longUrl}. Generate a unique ID (a Snowflake ID or a range-allocated counter), encode it in base62 (62^7 ≈ 3.5 trillion codes), and store code → longUrl, owner and expiry in a key-value store.

Read path: GET /{code} goes through the CDN or edge, then a load balancer to stateless services, then a Redis cache, then the key-value store on a miss. Answer with a 301 (cacheable, cheapest) or 302 (every click reaches you, so you can count it).
Publish click events asynchronously to a stream for analytics. Never do it inline on the redirect.
Rate-limit creation per user or IP to stop spam, and check URLs against a malware list.

sections.title: Trade-offs to discuss
items: Hash of the URL plus a collision check makes duplicate URLs share one code, but costs a read on every write.
A counter per range (each server leases blocks of 1,000 IDs) needs no coordination per request.
Custom aliases require a uniqueness check, for example a conditional put.

cards.title: News Feed / Timeline
cards.subtitle: Like Twitter/X, Instagram or Facebook
cards.lego: Every follower has a personal mailbox tray. Do you drop a copy of each new brick into every tray (push), or does each follower walk around collecting bricks when they look (pull)?
cards.summary: Users follow others and open their home timeline: the newest posts from everyone they follow, loaded in under 200 ms. Some accounts have 100 million followers.
steps: Post service: store the post in a sharded store (by author) and media in object storage behind a CDN.
Publish PostCreated to a queue or stream.
Fan-out workers look up the author's followers and push the post ID into each follower's timeline list in Redis (fan-out on write), trimmed to the newest ~800 IDs.
For celebrity authors, skip fan-out. At read time, merge their recent posts into the follower's cached timeline (fan-out on read). This hybrid approach is the classic answer.
The timeline read fetches IDs from Redis, hydrates the post bodies from the post cache or store, and ranks them.

sections.title: Why
items: Reads vastly outnumber writes, so precompute timelines to make reads cheap.
Pushing a celebrity's post to 100 million timelines would take far too long and cost too much, hence the hybrid.

sections.title: Break it
items: The fan-out queue backs up after a viral post: timelines lag. Prioritize active users and skip fan-out to dormant ones.
The timeline cache is lost: rebuild on demand from the social graph plus recent posts, and protect the database with request coalescing.

links.title: TAO: Facebook's Distributed Data Store for the Social Graph

cards.title: Real-Time Chat
cards.subtitle: Like WhatsApp, Slack or Discord
cards.lego: Each person keeps a walkie-talkie line open to a switchboard brick. The switchboard knows who's on which line and relays each message instantly.
cards.summary: One-to-one and group chat with messages delivered in under a second, online presence, message history, and delivery to offline users.
steps: Clients hold a persistent WebSocket to a fleet of connection-gateway servers behind an L4 load balancer.
A session registry in Redis maps user_id to the gateway that holds their connection, and tracks presence with heartbeats and TTLs.
When a message is sent, the chat service assigns a per-channel sequence number and persists it to a wide-column store partitioned by (channel_id, time bucket).
The message is published to a stream or pub/sub topic. The gateways holding recipients' connections push it down their sockets.
Offline recipients get a push notification through a notification queue, and clients sync missed messages on reconnect using their last seen sequence number.

sections.title: Break it
items: A gateway server dies: all its clients reconnect at once. Add jittered reconnect backoff, or they stampede the survivors.
A huge channel (a server with 1 million members) becomes a hot partition. Use time-bucketed partitions and fan out in tiers.
Duplicate sends on flaky mobile networks: a client message ID deduplicates them.

links.title: How Discord Stores Trillions of Messages

cards.title: Video Streaming
cards.subtitle: Like Netflix or YouTube
cards.lego: Chop each movie into small numbered bricks at several quality levels, stock copies in every corner shop, and let each viewer's player grab whichever size fits their connection.
cards.summary: Creators upload large video files, and millions of viewers worldwide stream them smoothly on connections ranging from 3G to fibre.
steps: The client asks the API for a presigned URL and uploads the raw file directly to object storage in multiple parts.

The upload event triggers a transcoding pipeline: a queue of jobs split into chunks that workers encode in parallel into many bitrates and resolutions, packaged as HLS or DASH segments of about 2–6 seconds.
Segments and manifests are written back to object storage, and metadata (title, status, segment locations) goes to a database.
Viewers fetch the manifest and segments from a CDN. The player's adaptive bitrate logic switches quality segment by segment as bandwidth changes.
Views, watch time and quality-of-experience events stream into analytics and recommendations.

sections.title: Break it
items: A new episode drops and the CDN is cold: pre-position popular titles at the edge before release.
A transcode worker dies mid-chunk: the job becomes visible again and is re-encoded. Writes to deterministic output keys make that idempotent.

links.title: Netflix Open Connect
links.note: The CDN appliances Netflix places inside ISPs

cards.title: Distributed Rate Limiter
cards.subtitle: Protect an API used by millions of clients
cards.lego: A turnstile at every entrance, all reading the same shared tally board so no one can sneak extra passes by switching doors.
cards.summary: Limit each API key to N requests per minute across a fleet of 200 gateway nodes, adding less than 1–2 ms of latency, and keep the API up even if the limiter's store has trouble.
steps: Enforce in the API Gateway or a sidecar, before the request reaches business services.
Keep a token bucket per key in Redis, updated atomically with a Lua script that refills based on elapsed time and takes one token.
Shard the Redis keys by API key. Hot keys can keep a small local token cache on each gateway, synced asynchronously.
Reject with 429 Too Many Requests, a Retry-After header, and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers.
Choose deliberately what happens when Redis is unreachable: fail open, with a coarse local limit as a backstop.

sections.title: Algorithms
items: Token bucket: allows bursts and is simple. Sliding-window counter: smooth and memory-cheap. Fixed window: simplest, but allows double bursts at the edges.

links.title: Scaling your API with rate limiters
How we built rate limiting capable of scaling to millions of domains

cards.title: Notification System
cards.subtitle: Push, SMS and email at scale
cards.lego: A mailroom that sorts every outgoing letter into the right chute (push, SMS or email), throws out duplicates, and keeps retrying any letter the post office bounces.
cards.summary: Many product services need to notify users through push, SMS and email: tens of millions of messages a day, respecting user preferences, never double-sending, and surviving flaky third-party providers.
steps: Services call a Notification API (or publish events) with user_id, template and data, plus an idempotency key.
The notification service checks user preferences, quiet hours and rate caps, renders the template, and deduplicates on the key.
It enqueues onto a separate queue per channel (push, SMS, email) so a slow SMS provider can't block push.
Channel workers call the providers (APNs/FCM, Twilio, SES) with timeouts, retries with backoff, and circuit breakers per provider, failing over to a secondary provider where possible.
Messages that exhaust their retries go to a dead-letter queue. Delivery status streams into analytics.

sections.title: Break it
items: The email provider is down for an hour: the email queue grows while push and SMS keep flowing, and the backlog drains when the provider recovers. Set a TTL for time-sensitive messages such as one-time passcodes.
A marketing blast of 50 million messages starves transactional ones: use separate priority queues.

links.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

cards.title: System Design Primers
cards.subtitle: ByteByteGo System Design 101 · The System Design Primer
cards.lego: The official instruction booklets. Flip through every page once before you try your own model.
cards.summary: Two free, visual, community-maintained overviews of every standard brick and pattern. ByteByteGo's System Design 101 is a collection of one-page diagrams (how HTTPS works, CDN, caching and database choices). Donne Martin's System Design Primer is a structured syllabus with worked solutions and Anki decks.

sections.title: How to study them
items: Read one topic, close the tab, and redraw the diagram from memory in Excalidraw. Compare, then fix the gaps.
Map each topic to a card in this app, and put anything new in the card's Notes (N).

cards.title: System Design Interview, Volumes 1 & 2
cards.subtitle: Alex Xu (and Sahn Lam for Volume 2)
cards.lego: The master-builder sets: complete models with step-by-step instructions and the reasoning behind each choice.
cards.summary: Chapter-length walkthroughs of the classic builds, including the rate limiter, consistent hashing, key-value store, unique ID generator, URL shortener, web crawler, notification system, news feed, chat, search autocomplete, YouTube and Google Drive. Volume 2 adds proximity search, maps, payments, a stock exchange and more. Each follows a four-step framework: scope the problem, propose a high-level design, deep dive, wrap up.

sections.title: How to study it
items: Before each chapter, give yourself 45 minutes to design it cold. Then read it and list what you missed.
Rebuild the chapter's design as a Build card in your notes, with its steps and the bricks used.

cards.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications
cards.subtitle: Martin Kleppmann (O'Reilly)
cards.lego: The materials-science textbook: why each kind of plastic bends, snaps or holds under load.
cards.summary: The deepest single book on the principles under the bricks: storage engines (LSM trees vs B-trees), encoding, replication, partitioning, transactions and isolation levels, the trouble with distributed systems, consistency and consensus, and batch and stream processing. It is where interview answers turn into real understanding.

sections.title: How to study it
items: One chapter a week. After each, write a one-paragraph explanation in Notes as if teaching a junior engineer.
Follow the chapter references into the papers listed under Foundational Papers.

cards.title: Netflix: Datacenter Monolith → Cloud Microservices
cards.subtitle: Netflix Tech Blog
cards.lego: Watching a master builder take apart one giant brittle model and rebuild it as hundreds of small, replaceable sub-assemblies, while it stays on display the whole time.
cards.summary: In 2008 a major database corruption stopped DVD shipments for three days. Netflix then spent about seven years moving from a monolith in its own datacenters to hundreds of microservices on AWS, finishing in 2016. Along the way it invented or popularized chaos engineering (Chaos Monkey), client-side load balancing, circuit breakers (Hystrix) and its own CDN (Open Connect).

sections.title: What to take away
items: Migrate incrementally: move one service or dataset at a time, with dual running and rollbacks.
Design for failure as the normal state, then prove it continuously in production.

cards.title: Uber: Monolith → Microservices → Domains
cards.subtitle: Uber Engineering blog
cards.lego: Too many tiny sub-assemblies became impossible to navigate, so they were regrouped into labelled domains with a single door each.
cards.summary: Uber split its early Python monolith into thousands of microservices to scale teams and cities. The complexity that followed led to Domain-Oriented Microservice Architecture (DOMA): services grouped into domains and layers, each behind a gateway. Uber also moved from Postgres to MySQL for replication at scale, built the Schemaless datastore, and created H3 for geospatial indexing.

sections.title: What to take away
items: Microservices solve organizational scaling but create operational complexity, so group them deliberately.
Choose databases for their operational behaviour at scale (replication, upgrades), not just their features.

links.title: Why Uber Engineering switched from Postgres to MySQL
H3: Uber's Hexagonal Hierarchical Spatial Index

cards.title: Airbnb: Monorail → Service-Oriented Architecture
cards.subtitle: The Airbnb Tech Blog
cards.lego: One huge model everyone was editing at once got divided into owned sections with clear connection points.
cards.summary: Airbnb's Ruby on Rails monolith ('Monorail') slowed hundreds of engineers who were deploying the same codebase. Over several years Airbnb migrated to a service-oriented architecture, with presentation, mid-tier and data services, an IDL-based service framework, and strict ownership. It also wrote widely read posts on payments idempotency and data infrastructure.

sections.title: What to take away
items: Carve out services along data ownership. A service should own its tables.
Invest in the platform (service framework, schemas, observability) before the migration, not after.

links.title: The Airbnb Tech Blog
links.note: Search for 'Building Services at Airbnb' and 'Avoiding Double Payments'

cards.title: The Counterpoint: When Not to Split
cards.subtitle: Segment's 'Goodbye Microservices'
cards.lego: Sometimes the best build is fewer, larger bricks.
cards.summary: Segment split its event-delivery pipeline into more than 140 per-destination microservices and queues. Operational load, library drift and on-call pain grew until it merged them back into one service with better testing. The lesson: architecture follows constraints (team size, traffic, change rate). A well-structured modular monolith is a legitimate end state.

sections.title: Ask before splitting
items: Do the parts need to scale, deploy or fail independently? Are different teams blocked on each other?
Can a module boundary inside one deployable give 80% of the benefit?

links.title: Goodbye Microservices: From 100s of problem children to 1 superstar

cards.title: Google SRE Book & Amazon Builders' Library
cards.subtitle: Free, production-hardened operating manuals
cards.lego: The notes from people who keep the world's largest models standing day after day.
cards.summary: Google's Site Reliability Engineering book (free online) covers SLOs, overload handling, cascading failures, load balancing and incident response. The Amazon Builders' Library is a set of essays by Amazon principal engineers on timeouts and retries, load shedding, caching, health checks, static stability and shuffle-sharding. Together they are the best free source on how systems behave under failure.

sections.title: Start with
items: SRE book: Service Level Objectives, Handling Overload, Addressing Cascading Failures.
Builders' Library: Timeouts, retries and backoff with jitter; Using load shedding; Caching challenges and strategies.

cards.title: The Google File System (2003)
cards.subtitle: Ghemawat, Gobioff, Leung · SOSP 2003
cards.lego: The first mega storage bin built from thousands of cheap, breakable boxes.
cards.summary: A single master holds metadata; chunkservers store 64 MB chunks, each replicated three times. The design assumes component failure is normal, optimizes for large sequential reads and record appends, and relaxes consistency. It is the ancestor of HDFS and of modern object and blob storage.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Separate the metadata path (the master) from the data path (clients talk directly to chunkservers).
Leases give one replica authority to order mutations.

cards.title: MapReduce (2004)
cards.subtitle: Dean & Ghemawat · OSDI 2004
cards.lego: Give a thousand builders one simple instruction each, then gather their results in a sorted pile.
cards.summary: A programming model in which users write map (emit key-value pairs) and reduce (combine the values for each key), and the framework handles partitioning, scheduling, fault tolerance (re-running failed tasks) and stragglers (backup tasks). It launched Hadoop and the era of batch data processing.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Move computation to the data. Deterministic tasks can simply be re-executed on failure.

links.title: MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters (PDF)

cards.title: Bigtable (2006)
cards.subtitle: Chang et al. · OSDI 2006
cards.lego: The first giant Bionicle: a sparse, sorted, ever-growing map split into tablets.
cards.summary: A sparse, distributed, persistent, sorted map indexed by (row, column, timestamp). Tables split into tablets served by tablet servers; data is stored as SSTables on GFS, with Chubby for coordination. It inspired HBase and Cassandra's data model, and LSM-tree storage is now everywhere.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Write to a memtable and commit log, flush to immutable SSTables, and compact in the background. That is the LSM tree.
Row keys sorted lexicographically make row-key design the performance lever.

links.title: Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data (PDF)

cards.title: Dynamo (2007)
cards.subtitle: DeCandia et al. (Amazon) · SOSP 2007
cards.lego: A shopping-cart store that would rather show a slightly old cart than no cart at all.
cards.summary: An always-writable, highly available key-value store for Amazon's shopping cart. It combines consistent hashing with virtual nodes, replication to N nodes with tunable R and W quorums, sloppy quorums and hinted handoff, vector clocks for conflict detection, Merkle trees for anti-entropy, and gossip for membership. It shaped Cassandra, Riak and the NoSQL movement.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Availability over consistency for business reasons: an 'add to cart' must never fail.
Push conflict resolution to reads, and to the application.

links.title: Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store (PDF)
Amazon DynamoDB (USENIX ATC 2022)
links.note: How the managed service differs from the 2007 design

cards.title: The Log & Kafka (2011–2013)
cards.subtitle: Jay Kreps (LinkedIn)
cards.lego: The realization that the conveyor belt itself is the most important piece in the factory.
cards.summary: An essay arguing that an append-only, totally ordered log is the unifying abstraction behind databases (write-ahead logs), replication, data integration and stream processing. Built at LinkedIn as Kafka, it became the backbone of event-driven architectures and change data capture.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Put every change on a log, and every other system becomes a materialized view of it.
Each consumer tracks its own offset, which is why a stream can replay and a queue can't.

links.title: The Log: What every software engineer should know about real-time data's unifying abstraction

cards.title: Spanner (2012)
cards.subtitle: Corbett et al. (Google) · OSDI 2012
cards.lego: A rigid LEGO grid stretched across the whole planet, kept in sync by atomic clocks.
cards.summary: A globally distributed database with externally consistent (linearizable) transactions. TrueTime exposes clock uncertainty from GPS and atomic clocks, and commits wait out that uncertainty. Data is split into Paxos-replicated groups, and two-phase commit runs across groups. It showed that SQL, strong consistency and global scale can coexist, which inspired CockroachDB and YugabyteDB.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Bounded clock uncertainty plus commit-wait gives global ordering without a single leader.

cards.title: Raft & Paxos: Consensus
cards.subtitle: Ongaro & Ousterhout 2014 · Lamport 2001
cards.lego: The rule five builders use to agree on the next brick even when some of them fall asleep.
cards.summary: Consensus lets a cluster agree on an ordered log despite crashes, as long as a majority is up. Raft splits the problem into leader election, log replication and safety, and was designed to be understandable. It powers etcd (Kubernetes), Consul and CockroachDB. Paxos is the original, and 'Paxos Made Simple' is its short explanation.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Majority quorums: 5 nodes tolerate 2 failures. Terms (epochs) fence off stale leaders.

links.title: In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Raft)

cards.title: Scaling Memcache at Facebook (2013)
cards.subtitle: Nishtala et al. · NSDI 2013
cards.lego: How to run the world's biggest arm's-reach shelf without letting it lie to you.
cards.summary: How Facebook ran thousands of memcached servers serving billions of requests per second. The paper covers look-aside caching, leases that prevent stale sets and stampedes, regional pools, cold-cluster warm-up, and cross-region invalidation driven by the MySQL commit log. It is the practical manual for caching at scale.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Invalidate by deleting, never by setting, and drive deletions from the database's commit log.
Leases solve both stale sets and thundering herds.

cards.title: The Tail at Scale (2013)
cards.subtitle: Jeffrey Dean & Luiz André Barroso · CACM
cards.lego: In a model with a thousand pieces, the slowest piece sets the pace.
cards.summary: In a fan-out service, rare slow responses (the p99 tail) become the common case for users. The paper catalogues the causes (shared resources, garbage collection, queueing) and techniques to tolerate them: hedged requests, tied requests, micro-partitioning, selective replication, and putting slow machines on probation.

sections.title: Key ideas
items: Don't try to eliminate variability. Build systems that are tail-tolerant.

cards.title: Virtual CAD Tools for Architecture
cards.subtitle: Excalidraw · Miro · Eraser · draw.io · the C4 model
cards.lego: Digital LEGO Designer: lay out the whole model on screen before you buy a single brick.
cards.summary: Sketch system topologies before spending money on cloud infrastructure. Excalidraw has a fast hand-drawn feel and is great for interviews. Miro is a collaborative whiteboard. Eraser turns text into diagrams (diagram-as-code) and has cloud icons. draw.io is free and precise. The C4 model gives you zoom levels (context, containers, components, code) so diagrams stay readable.

sections.title: Practice routine
items: For every Build card, draw it from memory in under 10 minutes, then compare it with the card.
Use one colour per brick family, matching this app: compute orange, storage blue, networking green, glue purple.
Label each arrow with the protocol and whether it is synchronous or asynchronous.

cards.title: Map the Traffic Flow
cards.subtitle: Four questions for every diagram
cards.lego: Trace one peg's journey through the whole model with your finger.
cards.summary: Take any system you use (a food-delivery app, your company's checkout, this flashcard app) and draw a single request's journey from the user's thumb to durable storage and back.
steps: Where does data enter? DNS, the CDN or edge, the load balancer or API gateway. Mark auth and rate limiting here.
Where is it computed? Which stateless services handle it, and which calls are synchronous?
Where does it halt? Queues and streams: what is buffered, for how long, and who drains it?
Where is it cached? Browser, CDN, the Redis tier, in-process. For each, what TTL and how it is invalidated.
Where is it permanently saved? The source-of-truth database or object store, how it is replicated, and how it is backed up.
Finally, circle every single point of failure in red and write the fix next to it.

sections.title: Self-check
items: Can you say the p99 latency budget of each hop?
What happens to an in-flight request if each box dies right now?

cards.title: The 45-Minute Design Framework
cards.subtitle: From a blank page to a defended design
cards.lego: The instruction-booklet order: sort the pieces, build the base, add the details, then stress-test.
cards.summary: You're handed a vague prompt like 'Design Instagram' and a whiteboard. Walk through a repeatable sequence that produces a scoped, estimated, defensible design in about 45 minutes.
steps: Requirements (5 minutes): the functional core (3–5 features) and the non-functional targets: scale, latency, availability, and the consistency each feature needs.
Estimates (5 minutes): users, read and write QPS, peak, and storage per year. Decide whether it is read-heavy or write-heavy.
API (5 minutes): the main endpoints or events, with request and response shapes and idempotency.
Data model (5 minutes): entities, access patterns, and the choice between SQL and NoSQL, with the partition key.
High-level design (10 minutes): snap the bricks together and trace the read path and the write path.
Deep dive (10 minutes): the hardest part, such as fan-out, hot keys, consistency or matching. Offer alternatives and choose one.
Wrap-up (5 minutes): bottlenecks, failure modes, monitoring and alerting, and what you'd build next.

sections.title: Habits of strong candidates
items: State the trade-offs out loud: 'I'm choosing X over Y because…'
Start simple, then evolve: a single server, then the scaled version.

links.title: The System Design Primer: How to approach a system design interview question

cards.title: Project 1: Build a URL Shortener
cards.subtitle: API endpoint + hash generator + fast key-value store
cards.lego: Your first real MOC: three bricks and one working model on your own table.
cards.summary: Ship a working URL shortener on a free tier: POST a long URL and get a short code; GET the code and get redirected. Then measure it and make it faster.
steps: Compute: one HTTP service (a Cloudflare Worker, AWS Lambda behind a function URL or API Gateway, or a container on Fly.io or Cloud Run).
ID generator: base62-encode a counter (Redis INCR) or a random 7-character code with a conditional insert to reject collisions.
Key-value store: Upstash Redis, DynamoDB (on-demand), or Cloudflare KV storing code → URL.
Add caching: in-process LRU or edge cache headers for hot codes. Compare 301 and 302.
Add rate limiting per IP on POST and a click counter that is sent asynchronously (a queue or waitUntil).
Load-test it with k6 or hey. Record p50 and p99 before and after the cache in Notes (N).

sections.title: Stretch goals
items: Custom aliases with a uniqueness guarantee. Expiring links using TTL.
A click analytics dashboard fed from an event stream.

cards.title: Project 2: Image Thumbnail Generator
cards.subtitle: Object storage → event → serverless → object storage
cards.lego: Drop a big picture brick in one bin and watch a tiny robot place a miniature copy in the next bin.
cards.summary: Upload an image to an object storage bucket. A background event notification triggers a serverless function that resizes it and saves the thumbnail to another bucket or prefix, all without a server of your own.
steps: Create two buckets (or prefixes): uploads/ and thumbnails/. Writing output to a different place prevents an infinite trigger loop.
Give the client a presigned PUT URL from a tiny API so the image goes straight to storage.
Configure an S3 event notification (ObjectCreated), optionally through SQS for buffering and retries, to invoke a Lambda function.
The function downloads the image, resizes it (Sharp or Pillow) to several sizes, and writes them under thumbnails/{key}.
Record metadata (the original key, sizes, status) in a table, and show a gallery that reads the thumbnails through a CDN.
Upload the same file twice and upload a corrupt file. Confirm idempotency and that failures land in a DLQ.

sections.title: Stretch goals
items: Upload 1,000 images at once and watch concurrency, throttling and cost.
Switch the trigger to EventBridge and fan out to a second consumer, such as image labelling.

links.title: Tutorial: Using an Amazon S3 trigger to create thumbnail images

cards.title: Project 3: Flash-Sale Order Queue
cards.subtitle: A mini version of Example B that you can break
cards.lego: Rebuild the toy-store ticket slot on your desk, then send a stampede at it.
cards.summary: Build a tiny checkout: an API that accepts orders with an idempotency key, a queue, and a worker that writes to Postgres at a controlled rate. Then load-test it with a simulated flash sale.
steps: API (container or function): validate the order, do an atomic stock reservation in Redis, and enqueue {order, idempotencyKey}.
Queue: SQS, RabbitMQ in Docker, or a Postgres table used with SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.
Worker: an INSERT with UNIQUE(idempotency_key), a fake payment call with random failures and delays, and an acknowledgement only on success.
Blast it with 50× normal load using k6. Watch queue depth, worker throughput and database connections.
Kill the worker mid-run and restart it. Verify there are no lost or duplicated orders.

sections.title: What you should observe
items: API latency stays flat while the queue absorbs the spike.
The database's write rate stays at the worker's pace, not at the traffic's pace.

links.title: Designing robust and predictable APIs with idempotency

cards.title: Chaos Engineering
cards.subtitle: Break it on purpose, in daylight, with a hypothesis
cards.lego: Deliberately pull a brick out of your model to see whether it wobbles, holds, or collapses, before a child's elbow does it for you.
cards.summary: Chaos engineering means experimenting on a system to build confidence that it withstands turbulent conditions. Define the steady state (for example successful checkouts per minute), form a hypothesis ('if a cache node dies, checkouts stay within 5%'), inject a real-world fault, keep the blast radius small, and compare. Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly terminates production instances so teams must design for it.

sections.title: Fault menu
items: Kill an instance, container or availability zone. Crash or fail over the database.
Add latency or packet loss, fill the disk, exhaust connections, skew the clock, revoke credentials.

sections.title: Tools
items: Toxiproxy (latency and timeouts between services), tc netem (network faults on Linux), Chaos Mesh (Kubernetes), AWS Fault Injection Service.

links.title: Chaos Engineering (Basiri et al., IEEE Software 2016)

cards.title: Drill: The Database Crashes
cards.subtitle: Does the app fail gracefully, or fall over completely?
cards.lego: Yank out the bottom drawer while builders are still reaching into it.
cards.summary: With your mini-project under steady load, stop the primary database (docker stop postgres, or trigger a managed failover). Observe what happens to incoming traffic, then patch the holes.
steps: Write the hypothesis: 'Reads keep working from cache or a replica, writes queue up, and there are no 500s at the edge.'
Start load (k6 at a steady rate) and a dashboard of error rate, p99 latency and queue depth.
Kill the database. Watch: do requests hang (no timeout), return 500s instantly, or degrade?
Restore it. Watch: does the app reconnect on its own, or does it need a restart because the connection pool is dead?
Patch and repeat until the result matches the hypothesis.

sections.title: What should happen
items: Short connect and query timeouts, so there are no thread pile-ups.
The circuit breaker opens: serve cached reads and show a friendly 'saving…' for queued writes.
The health check stays shallow, so the load balancer doesn't eject every app server because the database is down.

sections.title: Common holes
items: No timeout (a default of infinity), connection pools that never re-validate, and retry storms on recovery.

cards.title: Drill: The Cache Layer Goes Down
cards.subtitle: Does the backend drown in database calls?
cards.lego: The arm's-reach shelf collapses, and suddenly every builder is digging in the heavy bottom drawer at once.
cards.summary: With your app serving a read-heavy load at a 95%+ cache hit rate, stop Redis, or flush it, to simulate a cold restart. Measure how much load hits the database and whether it survives.
steps: Record the baseline: the cache hit ratio, database QPS and database CPU.
Flush or stop the cache under load, and watch database QPS jump by roughly 1 / (1 − hit rate). A 95% hit rate means about 20× the load.
Note whether the database saturates, latency explodes, or the app times out and retries, which makes it worse.
Patch it: request coalescing (single-flight), a short in-process L1 cache, load shedding on low-priority reads, and gradual cache warming.
Repeat, and confirm the database stays under about 70% CPU during a cold start.

sections.title: The lesson
items: A cache that the database can't survive without is really a hidden dependency. Size the database for the cold-cache case, or protect it.

cards.title: Drill: Inject Artificial Latency
cards.subtitle: A slow dependency is worse than a dead one
cards.lego: One builder in the chain starts working in slow motion. Does the line wait politely, or does everyone pile up behind them?
cards.summary: Add 500 ms to 2 s of latency (and some packet loss) between your service and one dependency, such as payments or the database, using Toxiproxy or tc netem. Observe thread and connection exhaustion and cascading slowness.
steps: Put Toxiproxy between the app and the dependency, and add a latency toxic of 1,000 ms ± 300 ms.
Watch in-flight requests, pool usage and p99 latency upstream. Do unrelated endpoints slow down too?
Add timeouts (from the dependency's p99), bulkheads (a separate pool), and a circuit breaker with a fallback.
Add retries with capped exponential backoff and jitter, and check that they don't amplify the load.
Repeat, and confirm unrelated endpoints stay fast and the affected feature degrades cleanly.

sections.title: The lesson
items: Dead dependencies fail fast. Slow ones hold resources until everything is stuck. Timeouts are the first line of defence.

links.title: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter

cards.title: Drill: Poison Message & Queue Backlog
cards.subtitle: When the buffer tray overflows
cards.lego: One malformed piece jams the machine, and the tray behind it keeps filling up.
cards.summary: In your order-queue project, publish a message that always makes the worker throw an error, then double the producer rate beyond worker capacity for 10 minutes. See what happens to the queue, and to your users.
steps: Send the poison message. Does it retry forever and block a worker? Configure maxReceiveCount and a DLQ.
Alert on DLQ depth greater than zero, and build a redrive or replay path once the bug is fixed.
Overload the producers. Chart queue depth and the age of the oldest message against time.
Autoscale workers on backlog per worker, capped at the database's safe limit, and shed or delay low-priority messages.
Decide what the user sees when the ETA exceeds a threshold: an honest wait time, or reject at the edge.

sections.title: The lesson
items: Queues hide overload until they don't. Monitor the age of the oldest message, not just the count.

cards.title: Drill: Lose an Availability Zone
cards.subtitle: Static stability
cards.lego: Knock an entire table over. Does the model on the other tables keep standing without any rebuilding?
cards.summary: Simulate losing one of three availability zones: terminate its instances, and block its subnets or database replica. Can the remaining zones carry full traffic without any control-plane action, such as launching new instances?
steps: Pre-provision about 50% headroom per zone (with 3 zones, each runs at ≤ 66% so 2 zones can carry 100%).
Fail the zone: the load balancer health checks eject its targets, and the database fails over to a standby in another zone.
Measure the error spike duration, the failover time of the database and cache, and whether autoscaling was needed.
Verify there are no cross-zone hard dependencies, such as a single NAT gateway or a single-zone cache.
Write up the recovery time actually measured compared with your target, in Notes (N).

sections.title: The lesson
items: Design so that surviving a failure never requires the control plane to be healthy.

cards.title: Stream Processing
cards.subtitle: Apache Flink · Spark Structured Streaming · Kafka Streams · Google Dataflow (Beam)
cards.lego: Robots standing beside the conveyor belt that sort, count and combine pieces as they fly past, instead of waiting for the belt to stop.
cards.summary: Stream processing runs continuous computations over unbounded event streams: filters, enrichments, joins, and windowed aggregations (tumbling, sliding, session). Event time vs processing time matters. Watermarks estimate when a window has seen all its data, and allowed lateness plus triggers decide what to do with stragglers. State (counts, joins) lives in local stores such as RocksDB, and periodic distributed snapshots (Flink checkpoints) give exactly-once state on failure.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Real-time features (clicks in the last 5 minutes), fraud detection, live dashboards, inventory and price propagation, alerting.
Continuously materializing views into a cache, a search index or an OLAP store.

sections.title: Trade-offs
items: Harder to test and operate than batch. State migrations and reprocessing need planning.
Exactly-once holds end to end only with transactional or idempotent sinks.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Backpressure from a slow sink stalls the whole job and consumer lag grows.
State grows without bound from joins with no TTL, and checkpoints get slower and slower.
A skewed key (one mega-merchant) pins one task while the others idle.

links.title: Lightweight Asynchronous Snapshots for Distributed Dataflows
Structured Streaming: A Declarative API for Real-Time Applications in Apache Spark (SIGMOD 2018)

cards.title: Change Data Capture (CDC)
cards.subtitle: Debezium · Datastream · Netflix DBLog · Kafka Connect
cards.lego: A camera pointed at the database's diary, copying every line to the conveyor belt the moment it's written.
cards.summary: CDC tails the database's replication log (Postgres WAL, MySQL binlog) and emits every insert, update and delete as an ordered event, usually into Kafka. Downstream systems (search index, cache invalidation, data lake, feature store) stay in sync without dual writes from the application. An initial snapshot plus the ongoing log gives a complete copy.

sections.title: Use it for
items: Feeding the lakehouse and BigQuery in near-real time, invalidating caches, updating search indexes, publishing outbox events.

sections.title: Watch out
items: Schema changes flow downstream. Use a schema registry with compatibility rules.
Replication slots that aren't consumed make the source database retain WAL until its disk fills.

links.title: DBLog: A Watermark Based Change-Data-Capture Framework

cards.title: Lambda vs Kappa Architecture
cards.subtitle: Batch plus speed layer, or one streaming path with replay
cards.lego: Build the model twice (a careful overnight version plus a quick live sketch), or build it once on the conveyor belt and simply rewind the belt when you need to rebuild.
cards.summary: The Lambda architecture runs a batch layer (accurate, recomputed daily) and a speed layer (approximate, real time), and merges them at query time. The cost is two codebases that drift apart. The Kappa architecture uses a single stream-processing path over a replayable log (Kafka with long retention, or a lakehouse table), and reprocesses by replaying into a new version of the job. Modern stacks often blend the two: streaming for freshness, and a lakehouse where batch and streaming read and write the same tables.

sections.title: Choose
items: Lambda when batch logic is heavy (large ML training features) and a streaming approximation is acceptable.
Kappa when one codebase and one source of truth matter more, and replay is affordable.

links.title: The Log: What every software engineer should know

cards.title: Apache Spark
cards.subtitle: Spark SQL / DataFrames · Dataproc · Databricks · EMR
cards.lego: A crew of a hundred builders who each take a pile of pieces, sort them in parallel, swap pieces with each other when needed, and hand back one finished model.
cards.summary: A distributed compute engine. A driver turns your DataFrame or SQL code into a DAG of stages. Narrow transformations (map, filter) run in parallel per partition; wide ones (groupBy, join) shuffle data across the network between stages. The Catalyst optimizer and Tungsten execution engine generate efficient plans, and Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) re-plans at runtime: it coalesces partitions, switches join strategies and splits skewed partitions. Spark reads and writes Parquet, ORC, Iceberg and Delta tables on GCS, S3 or HDFS, and also runs Structured Streaming and MLlib.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Batch ETL and ELT over GBs to PBs, feature engineering for training, large joins and aggregations, backfills.
Batch scoring, or preparing data for Ray and GPU training jobs.

sections.title: Performance levers
items: Avoid shuffles. Broadcast small tables in joins, and filter and project early (predicate pushdown into Parquet).
Right-size partitions (about 128–256 MB each). Fix skew with AQE skew joins or by salting hot keys.
Cache only what is reused. Use columnar formats and partition tables by date.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Executor OOM from skew or huge shuffles. Driver OOM from collect() on big data.
The small-files problem: thousands of tiny outputs slow every downstream job. Compact them.
Spot or preemptible executor loss causes recomputation. Enable graceful decommissioning and checkpoints for long lineages.

links.title: Spark SQL: Relational Data Processing in Spark (SIGMOD 2015)
Adaptive Query Execution: Speeding Up Spark SQL at Runtime

cards.title: Workflow Orchestration
cards.subtitle: Apache Airflow · Cloud Composer · Dagster · Argo Workflows
cards.lego: The foreman's schedule board: which crew builds which section, in what order, at what time, and what to redo when a section collapses.
cards.summary: An orchestrator defines pipelines as DAGs of tasks with dependencies, schedules them (cron, data-aware or event triggers), retries failures, backfills historical intervals, and records run state and lineage. Airflow (Cloud Composer on GCP) is the de facto standard. Dagster is asset-centric, and Argo runs Kubernetes-native steps. Tasks should call out to engines (Spark, BigQuery, Ray); the orchestrator coordinates, it doesn't compute.

sections.title: Best practices
items: Make every task idempotent and parameterized by the logical date: overwrite the partition for that date, never append blindly.
Keep DAG files lightweight (no heavy imports or queries at parse time). Pass pointers such as GCS paths between tasks, not data.
Use sensors or deferrable operators for upstream data, set SLAs and alerting, and cap concurrency so backfills don't overload the warehouse.

cards.title: Lakehouse Table Formats
cards.subtitle: Apache Iceberg · Delta Lake · Apache Hudi · BigLake
cards.lego: Adds an inventory ledger to the giant storage bins, so everyone agrees exactly which pieces make up version 42 of the model, even while others add pieces.
cards.summary: Open table formats put a transactional metadata layer (snapshots, manifests, a transaction log) over Parquet files in object storage. They provide ACID commits with concurrent writers, schema evolution, hidden partitioning, time travel ('as of' queries), row-level upserts and deletes (MERGE), and compaction. Spark, Flink, Trino and BigQuery can all share the same tables. That brings warehouse reliability to cheap lake storage.

sections.title: Use it for
items: Bronze/silver/gold (raw → cleaned → aggregated) zones on GCS or S3. Streaming upserts from CDC. Reproducible training sets through time travel.

sections.title: Maintenance
items: Compact small files, expire old snapshots, and clean up orphan files on a schedule. Otherwise metadata and storage costs balloon.

links.title: Delta Lake: High-Performance ACID Table Storage over Cloud Object Stores (VLDB 2020)
Lakehouse: A New Generation of Open Platforms (CIDR 2021)

cards.title: Columnar Formats & Warehouses
cards.subtitle: Parquet · ORC · BigQuery · Snowflake · Apache Pinot / Druid
cards.lego: Store all the red pieces together, all the blue pieces together, and so on, so a question about only red pieces never has to open the other drawers.
cards.summary: Columnar storage keeps each column contiguous and compressed (dictionary, run-length and bit-packing encodings), with min/max statistics per row group. Queries read only the columns they need and skip blocks that can't match. Warehouses such as BigQuery (built on Dremel) separate storage from compute and run massively parallel SQL. Real-time OLAP engines (Pinot, Druid, ClickHouse) serve sub-second analytics on fresh streaming data.

sections.title: Design tips
items: Partition by date and cluster or sort by common filter columns. Avoid SELECT * on wide tables because you pay per byte scanned.
Use a warehouse for analysts and BI. Use OLAP engines for user-facing, high-QPS dashboards.

links.title: Dremel: A Decade of Interactive SQL Analysis at Web Scale (VLDB 2020)

cards.title: Batch Pipeline Design Principles
cards.subtitle: Idempotency · backfills · late data · data quality · lineage
cards.lego: Instructions written so that any step can be redone from scratch on any day and produce exactly the same section of the model.
cards.summary: Reliable batch pipelines follow a few rules. Treat each run as a pure function of its input partitions: an idempotent overwrite of the output partition for the logical date. Keep raw data immutable so you can recompute anything. Make backfills a first-class operation. Handle late-arriving data by reprocessing a trailing window. Put data-quality checks (row counts, null rates, schema, freshness, distribution drift) as gates between stages. Record lineage so you know what to rerun when an upstream table is fixed.

sections.title: Checklist
items: Write to a staging location, validate, then atomically swap or commit (table-format commit or partition overwrite).
Use data contracts and a schema registry between producing and consuming teams.
Set freshness SLAs per table, with alerts before consumers notice.
Size for the backfill case: 90 days at once, with capped concurrency.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Append-only reruns double-count. Silent schema changes produce null columns. A job that 'succeeds' on empty input overwrites good data with nothing.

cards.title: Daily Batch ETL to the Lakehouse
cards.subtitle: GCS + Spark + Iceberg + Airflow + BigQuery
cards.lego: Every night the crew unloads the day's delivery trucks, sorts the pieces into labelled bins, checks nothing is broken, and updates the showroom by morning.
cards.summary: Every night, ingest the previous day's orders, clickstream and inventory snapshots (about 5 TB) from operational systems. Clean, join and aggregate them into analytics tables and ML training features, available by 6 AM with guaranteed correctness and the ability to backfill any day.
steps: Land raw data in a GCS bronze bucket partitioned by dt=YYYY-MM-DD: database exports or CDC from Kafka via Kafka Connect, plus event files. Raw data is immutable.
An Airflow (Cloud Composer) DAG runs per logical date, with sensors waiting for each upstream partition.
Spark jobs on Dataproc clean and deduplicate into silver Iceberg tables, using MERGE on business keys so reruns are idempotent.
Data-quality gates (row counts against the prior 7 days, null rates, schema, freshness) must pass. On failure, stop and alert rather than publish.
Gold aggregates and features are written as a partition overwrite for that date, then exposed to BigQuery as BigLake or external tables.
Publish a 'dataset ready' event (Pub/Sub or Kafka) that triggers downstream training and feature materialization. Lineage is recorded.

sections.title: Numbers
items: 5 TB a day of raw input over a 4-hour window needs about 350 MB/s sustained, which is roughly 50–100 executors depending on the transforms.

sections.title: Break it
items: An upstream table arrives 3 hours late: sensors wait, the freshness SLA alert fires, and the pipeline catches up without manual reruns.
A bug is found in the silver logic from last month: backfill 30 dates with capped concurrency. Every task overwrites its partition, so nothing is double-counted.

cards.title: Real-Time Clickstream Analytics
cards.subtitle: Kafka → Flink → OLAP + lakehouse
cards.lego: Count every visitor's footsteps as they walk through the store, and put the live tally on a big board at the entrance.
cards.summary: Show merchants live dashboards (views, add-to-carts and conversion per product in the last 1–60 minutes) over 500,000 events per second, while keeping the full history for batch analytics and ML.
steps: Web and app SDKs send events to a collector behind the edge and gateway, which validates the schema and produces to Kafka keyed by session or product.
A Flink job deduplicates by event ID, enriches from a cached product dimension, and computes event-time windowed aggregates with watermarks.
Aggregates are upserted into a real-time OLAP store (Pinot or Druid) that serves dashboard queries in under a second.
Raw events also stream into an Iceberg table on GCS (the lake sink) for nightly batch jobs and ML features.
Late events inside the allowed lateness update the windows. Later ones are fixed by the nightly batch recompute.

sections.title: Break it
items: Kill a Flink TaskManager: the job restores from its checkpoint and reprocesses from committed Kafka offsets, with no double counts because the sink upserts.
A viral product creates a hot key: pre-aggregate locally before the keyed shuffle.

cards.title: Drill: Bad Data & the Big Backfill
cards.subtitle: Break your batch pipeline on purpose
cards.lego: Sneak a box of wrong-coloured pieces into the delivery and see whether the night crew notices before the showroom opens.
cards.summary: In your batch pipeline, inject three faults: an empty upstream file, a column renamed upstream, and duplicated input records. Then run a 60-day backfill. Does bad data reach the gold tables and dashboards, and does the backfill overload anything?
steps: Hypothesis: quality gates block all three faults, and the backfill finishes under the concurrency cap without hurting production jobs.
Inject the empty file. The row-count check against the trailing average must fail the run before the overwrite.
Inject the schema rename. Schema validation or the data contract must fail loudly, not produce null columns.
Inject duplicates. MERGE or deduplication on business keys must keep the gold counts unchanged.
Run the 60-day backfill with max_active_runs capped, and watch warehouse slots, the Spark cluster and the freshness of today's run.

sections.title: The lesson
items: Batch failures are usually silent. A pipeline that errors is better than one that publishes wrong numbers.

cards.title: Feature Store
cards.subtitle: Feast · Vertex AI Feature Store · Tecton · Uber Michelangelo Palette
cards.lego: A labelled parts bin that the training crew and the live-build crew both draw from, so the model is trained on exactly the pieces it will see in production.
cards.summary: A feature store defines features once and serves them two ways. The offline store (BigQuery, Iceberg) provides point-in-time-correct historical values for training, meaning no future data leaks into past labels. The online store (Redis, Bigtable, Cassandra, DynamoDB) provides the latest values at millisecond latency for inference. Materialization jobs (batch from Spark, streaming from Flink or Kafka) keep the online store fresh. A registry makes features discoverable and reusable across teams.

sections.title: Why it exists
items: Training/serving skew: features computed differently in the notebook and in the service silently wreck accuracy.
Point-in-time joins: each training label must see features as they were at that timestamp.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Stale online features when a materialization job fails. Monitor feature freshness like any SLO.
Online-store hot keys (a popular item) and cold misses. Serve defaults and alert on the fallback rate.

links.title: Meet Michelangelo: Uber's Machine Learning Platform
links.note: Where the feature-store idea became mainstream

cards.title: MLflow
cards.subtitle: Experiment tracking · Model Registry · packaging · LLM tracing and evaluation
cards.lego: The lab notebook and the certified-parts shelf: every experimental build is recorded, and only approved models get a version label and move to the showroom.
cards.summary: MLflow tracks experiments (params, metrics, artifacts, code version) and packages models in a standard 'MLmodel' flavor format. Its Model Registry versions models with aliases such as @champion and @challenger, and records lineage back to the run and data. It also provides LLM tracing and evaluation for GenAI apps. The registry is the handoff point between training pipelines and serving (KServe, Triton, Ray Serve, vLLM).

sections.title: Patterns
items: CI/CD for models: a training pipeline registers a new version, evaluation gates promote it, and serving picks up the alias.
Keep training data snapshots (lakehouse time travel) linked to the run for reproducibility.

links.title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (NeurIPS 2015)

cards.title: Ray
cards.subtitle: Ray Core · Ray Data · Ray Train · Ray Serve · KubeRay
cards.lego: A universal connector brick that lets you turn any Python function into a crew of builders spread across dozens of machines and GPUs.
cards.summary: Ray is a distributed Python runtime. Tasks are stateless remote functions and actors are stateful workers, scheduled over a cluster with CPU and GPU resource awareness and an object store for passing data. On top of it: Ray Data streams heterogeneous CPU and GPU pipelines (ideal for batch inference), Ray Train does distributed training, Ray Tune does hyperparameter search, and Ray Serve does online model serving with composition and autoscaling. It runs on Kubernetes via KubeRay, and many LLM stacks use it for multi-node vLLM.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Python-native ML workloads that Spark handles poorly: GPU batch inference, RL, many-model training, LLM fine-tuning, multi-model serving graphs.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Object store spilling or OOM from oversized objects. Head node as a single point of failure (use GCS fault tolerance). Idle GPUs from an under-fed CPU preprocessing stage.

links.title: Ray: A Distributed Framework for Emerging AI Applications (OSDI 2018)

cards.title: ML Pipelines & Model Lifecycle
cards.subtitle: Kubeflow Pipelines · Vertex AI Pipelines · TFX · monitoring and drift
cards.lego: The assembly line from raw pieces to the showroom: prep, train, test, certify, ship, and keep watching whether customers still like it.
cards.summary: Production ML is a loop: ingest and validate data, compute features, train, evaluate against the current champion, register, deploy (shadow, canary, A/B), then monitor for data drift, prediction drift and business metrics, which triggers retraining. Pipelines as code (Kubeflow, Vertex AI, TFX) make every step reproducible and schedulable.

sections.title: Checklist
items: Data validation before training. Evaluation gates on sliced metrics, not just the global average.
Shadow traffic before a canary. Keep the previous model warm for instant rollback.
Log features and predictions at serving time to build the next training set (with a feedback loop).

links.title: MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in ML
The ML Test Score: A Rubric for ML Production Readiness

cards.title: LLM Inference Fundamentals
cards.subtitle: Prefill vs decode · KV cache · TTFT / TPOT · memory-bandwidth bound
cards.lego: The model reads the whole instruction booklet in one gulp (prefill), then adds one brick at a time (decode), keeping every page it has read open on the table (the KV cache).
cards.summary: Generation has two phases. Prefill processes the whole prompt in parallel. It is compute-bound and sets time-to-first-token (TTFT). Decode produces one token per step per sequence. It is memory-bandwidth-bound, because every step reads all the weights plus the KV cache, and it sets time-per-output-token (TPOT) or inter-token latency. The KV cache stores the attention keys and values of every past token. Its size is 2 × layers × kv_heads × head_dim × bytes × tokens, and it usually limits how many requests fit on a GPU. Throughput comes from batching many sequences so the weight reads are shared.

sections.title: Napkin math
items: An 8B model in FP16 is about 16 GB of weights. At about 3.3 TB/s (H100), a single sequence's decode is limited to roughly 200 tokens/s.
Llama-3-8B KV cache (32 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 head dim, FP16) is about 128 KB per token, so a 4k-token context is about 0.5 GB per request.
Key metrics: TTFT, TPOT or ITL, end-to-end latency, tokens/s per GPU, goodput (requests meeting their SLO), and KV cache utilization.

sections.title: Levers
items: Batch more (continuous batching), shrink the KV cache (GQA, FP8 KV), shrink the weights (quantization), reuse the KV cache (prefix caching), guess ahead (speculative decoding), and split phases (disaggregation).

cards.title: Continuous Batching & PagedAttention
cards.subtitle: Iteration-level scheduling · paged KV-cache memory
cards.lego: Instead of waiting for a whole tray of builds to finish, slot a new build into any seat the moment one finishes. And store every build's open pages in small numbered boxes, not one giant reserved shelf.
cards.summary: Static batching waits for the longest sequence, so the GPU idles. Continuous (in-flight) batching, from Orca, schedules at every decode iteration: finished sequences leave and new ones join immediately. PagedAttention (vLLM) stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks with a block table, like OS virtual memory. That nearly eliminates fragmentation, lets many more sequences fit, and enables copy-on-write sharing for parallel sampling and shared prefixes. Chunked prefill splits long prompts so they don't stall ongoing decodes.

sections.title: Tuning knobs
items: max_num_seqs and max_num_batched_tokens, gpu_memory_utilization, chunked prefill on or off, and the preemption mode (recompute or swap) when the KV cache runs out.

cards.title: vLLM
cards.subtitle: High-throughput open-source LLM inference engine
cards.lego: The standard motor brick for large models: snap in any open model and it runs fast on the GPUs you have.
cards.summary: vLLM is the most widely used open inference engine. It provides PagedAttention, continuous batching, chunked prefill, automatic prefix caching, speculative decoding, quantization (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, INT4), tensor, pipeline and expert parallelism, LoRA multiplexing, structured output, and an OpenAI-compatible server. It runs on NVIDIA, AMD, TPU and other accelerators. It exposes Prometheus metrics (TTFT, TPOT, KV cache usage, queue depth) that autoscalers and routers consume. llm-d, Ray Serve and KServe all build on it.

sections.title: Operate it
items: Size memory: weights plus KV cache (gpu_memory_utilization) plus activation headroom. Set max_model_len to what you really need.
Scale on queue depth and KV cache utilization rather than CPU. Use prefix-aware routing across replicas.
Cold starts: model weights are 10–100+ GB. Pre-pull images, cache weights on local NVMe or with GCS FUSE, and keep warm replicas.

cards.title: SGLang
cards.subtitle: RadixAttention · structured generation · high-performance serving runtime
cards.lego: A motor brick with a memory for shared instruction pages: if a thousand builds start with the same page, it keeps just one copy in a tree.
cards.summary: SGLang is a fast serving runtime plus a frontend language for LLM programs. RadixAttention keeps the KV cache in a radix tree so any shared prefix (system prompts, few-shot examples, multi-turn history, agent loops) is reused automatically with LRU eviction, and its scheduler is cache-aware. It offers a fast constrained-decoding engine for JSON and regex output, an overlapped CPU scheduler, and strong DeepSeek/MoE support (data-parallel attention, expert parallelism, prefill/decode disaggregation).

sections.title: vLLM or SGLang?
items: Both are production-grade and converging. Benchmark on your model, prompt mix and hardware. SGLang tends to shine with heavy prefix sharing and structured output.

cards.title: NVIDIA Triton Inference Server
cards.subtitle: Dynamic batching · model repository · ensembles · TensorRT-LLM backend
cards.lego: A multi-socket motor housing: plug in PyTorch, ONNX, TensorRT or Python models side by side and share one set of GPUs.
cards.summary: Triton serves models from many frameworks (TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, TensorFlow, Python, and TensorRT-LLM or vLLM for LLMs) out of a versioned model repository over HTTP or gRPC. The dynamic batcher groups incoming requests up to a max queue delay. Concurrent model instances share GPUs. Ensembles and BLS chain preprocessing, model and postprocessing steps. Model Analyzer finds the best batch and instance configuration. It exports Prometheus metrics and is deployed under KServe or directly on Kubernetes. NVIDIA Dynamo is its successor for large-scale distributed LLM serving.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Classic deep learning models (ranking, vision, embeddings) that need high QPS and low latency, multi-model GPU sharing, or NVIDIA-optimized TensorRT(-LLM) engines.

cards.title: Prefix Caching & KV-Aware Routing
cards.subtitle: Automatic prefix caching · cache-aware load balancing · KV offload tiers
cards.lego: Send each builder the jobs whose first instruction pages are already open on their table.
cards.summary: Prefix caching reuses KV blocks for identical prompt prefixes (system prompts, RAG context, chat history), cutting TTFT and prefill compute dramatically. The cache lives per replica, though, so a round-robin load balancer throws the hits away. KV-aware or prefix-aware routers (llm-d's inference scheduler, the Gateway API Inference Extension endpoint picker, Dynamo's KV router, SGLang's router) score replicas on cached-prefix overlap, queue depth and KV utilization. Tiered KV offload (GPU HBM → CPU RAM → local SSD → remote store, as in LMCache and Mooncake) extends the reusable cache further.

sections.title: Design tips
items: Put static content first in prompts (system prompt, tools, documents) and variable content last to maximize prefix hits.
Balance cache affinity against load: pure affinity creates hot replicas.

cards.title: Model Parallelism for Serving
cards.subtitle: Tensor · pipeline · expert · data parallelism
cards.lego: When the model is too big for one baseplate, split each layer across plates (tensor), stack layers on different plates (pipeline), or give each specialist its own plate (experts).
cards.summary: When the weights plus KV cache exceed one GPU, split the model. Tensor parallelism (TP) shards each layer's matrices across GPUs and all-reduces every layer, so it needs NVLink and should stay within a node. Pipeline parallelism (PP) puts consecutive layers on different GPUs or nodes; it needs less communication but adds bubbles and latency. Expert parallelism (EP) spreads mixture-of-experts experts across GPUs with all-to-all token routing. Data parallelism (DP) runs replicas. Typical choice: TP within a node, PP or EP across nodes, DP for throughput.

sections.title: Napkin math
items: A 70B model in FP16 is about 140 GB, so TP=4 on 80 GB GPUs leaves room for the KV cache. In FP8 it's about 70 GB, which fits TP=2 or a single 141 GB GPU.

links.title: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism

cards.title: Quantization
cards.subtitle: FP8 · INT8 · INT4 (AWQ, GPTQ) · KV cache quantization
cards.lego: Swap heavy bricks for lighter ones that look almost the same: the model fits on fewer baseplates and moves faster.
cards.summary: Quantization stores weights (and optionally activations and the KV cache) in fewer bits. Decode is memory-bandwidth-bound, so halving the bytes roughly doubles tokens per second and halves the GPUs needed. FP8 (Hopper and newer) is nearly lossless for most models. INT4 weight-only methods (AWQ, GPTQ) fit big models on small GPUs at some accuracy cost. A quantized KV cache doubles the concurrent context.

sections.title: Rule
items: Always evaluate on your own tasks after quantizing. Averaged benchmarks hide regressions on math, code and long context.

cards.title: Speculative Decoding
cards.subtitle: Draft models · Medusa · EAGLE · n-gram lookup
cards.lego: An apprentice quickly places the next few bricks, and the master checks them all in one glance, keeping the correct ones.
cards.summary: A cheap drafter (a small model, extra heads such as Medusa or EAGLE, or n-gram prompt lookup) proposes k tokens. The big model verifies all k in one forward pass, which costs about the same as one decode step because decode is memory-bound. Accepted tokens are kept, and the output distribution is mathematically unchanged. The result is 2–3× lower latency at low batch sizes. The gains shrink at high batch sizes, where the GPU is already compute-saturated.

sections.title: Use when
items: Latency-sensitive, low-to-moderate concurrency. Predictable output (code, extraction, RAG with copying) gets high acceptance rates.

cards.title: Disaggregated Prefill / Decode
cards.subtitle: DistServe · Splitwise · Mooncake · NVIDIA Dynamo · llm-d
cards.lego: One crew only reads instruction booklets and hands the open pages to a second crew that only places bricks, so neither slows the other down.
cards.summary: Prefill (compute-heavy, bursty) and decode (bandwidth-heavy, steady) interfere when colocated: a long prompt stalls everyone's next token. Disaggregation runs them on separate GPU pools, each with its own parallelism and batch sizes. The KV cache is transferred from prefill to decode workers over NVLink or RDMA (NIXL). The pools scale independently to meet TTFT and TPOT SLOs, which maximizes goodput. It pays off at large scale and with long prompts; for small deployments, chunked prefill is simpler.

sections.title: Costs
items: KV transfer bandwidth (high-speed interconnect required), more moving parts, and a router that must pair prefill and decode workers.

cards.title: Kubernetes Model Serving & GPU Autoscaling
cards.subtitle: KServe · Gateway API Inference Extension · llm-d · KEDA · GKE GPU node pools
cards.lego: The baseplate manager for motor bricks: it knows which plates have GPUs, adds plates when the queue grows, and parks idle ones.
cards.summary: On Kubernetes, model servers (vLLM, SGLang, Triton) run as Deployments or LeaderWorkerSets on GPU node pools. KServe provides an InferenceService abstraction with canary rollouts and scale-to-zero. The Gateway API Inference Extension (GAIE) adds model-aware routing (InferencePool, endpoint picker) to Envoy- or Istio-based gateways. llm-d combines vLLM, GAIE, KV-aware scheduling and disaggregation. Autoscale on inference signals (queue length, KV cache utilization, TTFT) via KEDA or custom metrics, not CPU.

sections.title: Gotchas
items: GPU scale-up is slow: node provisioning plus image pull plus weight load can take minutes. Keep headroom, use image streaming, and cache weights.
GPU scarcity: use reservations, multiple regions and zones, and fallback models. Bin-pack small models with MIG or time-slicing.

cards.title: AI Gateway
cards.subtitle: LiteLLM · Envoy AI Gateway · token rate limiting · fallbacks · guardrails
cards.lego: The front desk for every model: one entrance, a badge check, a token budget per team, and a detour when a model is down.
cards.summary: An AI gateway sits in front of self-hosted and vendor models behind a single OpenAI-compatible API. It handles authentication and per-team quotas measured in tokens (not requests), routing by model and cost, retries and fallbacks across providers, semantic or exact response caching, guardrails (PII redaction, safety filters), and usage metering. It streams responses (SSE) and logs prompts and completions for evaluation.

sections.title: Design tips
items: Rate-limit on estimated plus actual tokens. Set streaming-aware timeouts (on first token, and between tokens).
Fallback chain: self-hosted primary, then a smaller model, then a vendor API, then a graceful 'try later'.

cards.title: Multi-LoRA Serving
cards.subtitle: S-LoRA · Punica · LoRAX · vLLM LoRA adapters
cards.lego: One big motor with a rack of tiny snap-on attachments: every customer gets their own custom tool head without needing their own motor.
cards.summary: LoRA fine-tunes add small low-rank adapter matrices (a few MB to a few hundred MB) to a shared base model. A multi-LoRA server keeps one copy of the base weights on the GPU and batches requests for different adapters together, using custom kernels (Punica's SGMV, S-LoRA's unified paging) so mixed-adapter batches stay efficient. Adapters are loaded on demand from object storage into CPU and GPU caches with LRU eviction. Thousands of fine-tuned 'models' can share one GPU pool.

sections.title: Reach for it when
items: Fine-tuning as a service, per-customer or per-task specializations (per-merchant tone, per-language, per-domain), or A/B testing many fine-tunes cheaply.

sections.title: How it breaks
items: Cold adapter loads add latency spikes. Pre-warm popular adapters and route by adapter affinity.
Too many distinct adapters in one batch slows the kernels. Cap max_loras per batch.
Adapter and base-model version mismatch after a base upgrade. Pin versions in the registry.

cards.title: Structured Output & Tool Calling
cards.subtitle: Constrained decoding · JSON schema · grammars · XGrammar · Outlines
cards.lego: A stencil laid over the baseplate: the model can only place bricks where the stencil has holes, so the result always fits the socket it's going into.
cards.summary: Constrained decoding masks the model's next-token probabilities so the output must match a JSON schema, a regex or a context-free grammar. Downstream code, and tool calls in agents, never receive malformed output. Modern engines (XGrammar, Outlines, llguidance) precompile the grammar into token masks so the per-token overhead is negligible, and vLLM and SGLang expose it through OpenAI-style response_format and tool schemas.

sections.title: Design tips
items: Keep schemas small and flat. Deeply nested or huge enum schemas slow mask compilation, so cache compiled grammars per schema.
Constraints guarantee the shape, not correctness. Still validate the values and retry on semantic errors.
