cards.title: Token Streaming & Cancellation
cards.subtitle: Server-Sent Events · WebSockets · gRPC streams · WebRTC · request cancellation
cards.lego: Hand each brick to the customer the moment it's placed instead of shipping the finished model, and stop building the instant they walk away.
cards.summary: LLM responses are streamed token by token so perceived latency is the time to first token, not the full generation time. Chat APIs mostly use Server-Sent Events over HTTP. Bidirectional apps (voice, collaborative editing) use WebSockets or WebRTC. Every hop (CDN, gateway, service mesh, load balancer) must support long-lived streaming connections without buffering. A client disconnect must propagate to the engine so it frees the sequence's KV cache and stops wasting GPU time.

sections.title: Gotchas
items: Proxies that buffer responses (default nginx and some CDNs) destroy streaming. Disable buffering for these routes.
Idle and read timeouts must allow for long generations. Heartbeat comments keep connections alive.
Cancelled requests that keep decoding are a silent capacity leak. Monitor aborted versus completed requests.
Retries after partial output need care: resume or restart, and tell the client which.

cards.title: Inference Caching: Prompt, Exact & Semantic
cards.subtitle: Provider prompt caching · response caches · GPTCache · LMCache
cards.lego: Keep photos of models you've already built: if someone asks for the same model (or one that looks the same) you show them the photo instead of rebuilding.
cards.summary: There are three layers of reuse. Prompt (KV) caching reuses the computed attention state for a shared prefix, so answers stay fresh but prefill is skipped. Exact-response caching returns a stored completion for an identical request, which is safe only with deterministic settings (temperature 0) and non-personal content. Semantic caching embeds the query and returns a cached answer when a previous query is similar enough. It is cheap but risky: similar-looking questions can need different answers. Cross-instance KV caches (LMCache, Mooncake) share prefix state across replicas and tiers.

sections.title: Rules
items: Scope caches per tenant and per model version, and never serve one user's personal answer to another.
Tune semantic similarity thresholds on real traffic and track the false-hit rate, not just the hit rate.
Invalidate on model, prompt-template or source-data changes.

cards.title: Code Completion (Copilot-style)
cards.subtitle: Ghost-text suggestions on every keystroke
cards.lego: A builder watching over your shoulder who has to hand you the next brick before your hand reaches the pile, or not bother at all.
cards.summary: Suggest the next lines of code inline in the IDE for 1M active developers. Suggestions must appear within about 300 ms end to end or they are useless. Most requests are cancelled because the user keeps typing, and context (surrounding files) is large.
steps: The IDE plugin debounces keystrokes (about 50–100 ms), builds a fill-in-the-middle prompt (code before and after the cursor, plus snippets from open tabs and similar files), and caches recent completions locally.

Requests go to the nearest region over a persistent HTTP/2 connection (Torbit or CDN edge, then the AI gateway for auth and quotas). A new keystroke cancels the in-flight request all the way down to the engine.
A small, fast code model (1–15B, FP8) runs on vLLM or TensorRT-LLM with prefix caching. Consecutive requests from the same file share most of their prefix, so route by user or file affinity.
Speculative decoding with n-gram or prompt lookup is highly effective because code often copies nearby text. Cap output at a few lines and stop at the block end.
Post-filter suggestions (syntax check, duplicate and license filters) and stream the first lines as soon as they're ready.
Log accept, reject and partial-accept events to Kafka. The acceptance rate is the key product metric and feeds evaluation and fine-tuning.

sections.title: Numbers
items: Budget roughly 300 ms: about 50 ms network, about 100 ms prefill of a 2–4k-token prompt, about 100 ms for 20–40 output tokens with speculation, and the rest for the plugin.
With 1M developers at a few requests a minute, 30–60% are cancelled. Cancellation is a capacity feature, not an edge case.

sections.title: Break it
items: Disable cancellation propagation: GPU load jumps and p95 latency explodes, which shows why aborts must reach the engine.
Route round-robin instead of by affinity: the prefix-cache hit rate collapses and TTFT doubles.

cards.title: Fine-Tuning as a Service: Thousands of LoRA Models
cards.subtitle: One base model, 5,000 customer adapters, one GPU pool
cards.lego: Instead of a motor per customer, one row of motors with a wall of snap-on tool heads fetched as each order arrives.
cards.summary: Customers upload data, get a fine-tuned 'model' and call it by name. There are 5,000 fine-tunes, most rarely used and a few very hot. Dedicated GPUs per fine-tune would cost 5,000× too much; serve them all from a shared pool with p95 TTFT under 1 s.
steps: Fine-tuning jobs (Ray Train) produce LoRA adapters that are registered in MLflow with their base-model version and stored in GCS.
The AI gateway maps the customer model name to (base model, adapter ID) and enforces per-tenant token quotas.
An adapter-aware router sends a request to a replica that already has the adapter loaded, falling back to the least-loaded replica with free adapter slots.

vLLM or LoRAX replicas hold the base model once, keep hot adapters in GPU memory and warm ones in CPU memory, and fetch cold ones from GCS through a local disk cache. Mixed-adapter batches use SGMV kernels.
Very hot adapters are merged into dedicated replicas, and idle ones age out of every cache. Per-tenant metering feeds billing.

sections.title: Napkin
items: Llama-3-8B adapters at rank 16 on attention layers are about 20–50 MB each. 5,000 adapters is 100–250 GB total: too much for one GPU, easy for a CPU plus NVMe tier.

sections.title: Break it
items: A noisy tenant floods its adapter: per-tenant token-rate limits and fair queuing must protect the others.
Upgrade the base model: every adapter must be retrained or pinned to the old base. Run both bases side by side during migration.

cards.title: Real-Time Payment Fraud Scoring
cards.subtitle: Classic online inference in the checkout critical path
cards.lego: A security guard at the checkout who has 50 ms to look at the customer's history and decide: wave through, ask for ID, or stop.
cards.summary: Score every payment authorization (20,000 per second at peak) for fraud before approving it. The p99 must be under 50 ms because this is inside checkout, availability must be 99.99%, and new fraud patterns must be caught within minutes.
steps: The checkout service calls the scoring service synchronously with a strict timeout. On timeout, fall back to a rules-only decision rather than failing the payment.

The scoring service fetches features in one batched call: real-time velocity features (card attempts in the last 10 minutes, new device, amount versus the user's norm) from the online feature store (Redis or Cassandra), plus precomputed batch features.
Streaming features are maintained by Flink over the payment event stream in Kafka. Batch features come from nightly Spark jobs, materialized online.

The model is a gradient-boosted tree ensemble (CPU, or Triton's FIL backend), optionally combined with a small neural model. A rules engine applies hard blocks and allows. The output is approve, challenge (3-D Secure) or decline.

Every decision, with its features and model version, is logged to Kafka. Chargebacks arrive weeks later as labels for retraining. New models run in shadow, then canary, gated on precision, recall and dollars saved.

sections.title: Numbers
items: 50 ms p99 splits into about 5 ms network, 10–15 ms feature fetch (one round trip, parallel), 5–10 ms model, and the rest as headroom. No LLM fits this path.

sections.title: Break it
items: The feature store is slow: the timeout plus fallback to rules keeps checkout up. Alert on the fallback rate.
The streaming job lags: velocity features go stale and fraud slips through. Alert on feature freshness, not just latency.

cards.title: Semantic Product Search
cards.subtitle: Embedding service + ANN retrieval + cross-encoder reranker
cards.lego: Translate the shopper's words into coordinates on a map of all products, grab the nearest ones, and let an expert reorder the shortlist.
cards.summary: Improve search for 'shoes for a rainy hike' over 100M products at 30,000 queries per second with p95 under 150 ms, combining keyword and semantic matches.
steps: Offline: embed every product title and description with a batch job (Ray Data on GPUs), then build a sharded ANN index (HNSW or ScaNN) plus the keyword index. CDC and Kafka keep both fresh.

Online: the query goes to an embedding service (a small encoder on Triton or Text Embeddings Inference with dynamic batching; queries are short, so batches are large and cheap). Popular query embeddings are cached.
Run keyword search and ANN search in parallel, fetching about 200 candidates each, then fuse them (reciprocal rank fusion).
A cross-encoder reranker on GPU scores the top about 100 (query, product) pairs, and business rules (stock, sponsored slots) apply. Return the top 40.
Log queries, results and clicks. Evaluate offline with NDCG and online with A/B tests, and retrain the encoder on click data.

sections.title: Break it
items: The reranker pool is saturated: skip reranking (the degraded but fast path) instead of timing out the whole search.
An embedding model upgrade: new query vectors don't match the old index. Re-embed the corpus and swap indexes atomically (blue/green).

cards.title: Agentic Assistant with Tool Calling
cards.subtitle: Multi-turn, long-context, many model calls per user request
cards.lego: A builder who keeps going back to the parts catalog, the order system and the calculator, dozens of times, before handing you the finished model.
cards.summary: A customer-support agent that looks up orders, checks policies, issues refunds and answers in chat. One user turn can trigger 5–20 LLM calls with growing context (up to 50k tokens), and it must stay responsive and never take unsafe actions.
steps: Sessions are sticky: the gateway routes every call in a session to the same engine replica (or the KV-aware router finds it), so the ever-growing conversation prefix stays cached.

Each step's LLM call uses structured output (a JSON tool-call schema) on SGLang or vLLM. The orchestrator validates the arguments and executes the tool (order API, policy search, refund service) with idempotency keys and timeouts.

Tool results are appended to the context. Stable content (system prompt, tool definitions) sits at the front for maximum prefix reuse. Long sessions offload KV to CPU or SSD (LMCache) instead of recomputing.
Guardrails check risky actions (refunds above $X need confirmation or human approval), and every step is traced with OpenTelemetry (prompt, tool, latency, tokens).
Intermediate progress ('Checking your order…') streams to the user so perceived latency stays low. Cap steps and tokens per turn to bound cost.

sections.title: Numbers
items: Ten calls over a 30k-token context without prefix caching means about 300k prefill tokens per turn. With a 95% hit rate it's about 15k: a 20× cost difference.

sections.title: Break it
items: A tool hangs: the step timeout makes the agent tell the user rather than spin. A replica restart mid-session: KV is lost, so the next call re-prefills (slow, but correct).

cards.title: Real-Time Voice Assistant
cards.subtitle: Streaming speech-to-text → LLM → text-to-speech in under a second
cards.lego: Three builders passing bricks hand to hand so fast that the customer hears the answer start before they've finished blinking.
cards.summary: A phone and app voice assistant for order status and returns. Voice-to-voice latency must be under about 800 ms to feel natural, users interrupt ('barge in'), and 5,000 concurrent calls are expected at peak.
steps: Audio flows over WebRTC (or telephony via SIP) to a media server in the nearest region. Voice activity detection spots the end of the user's turn.
Streaming ASR (a Whisper-class or streaming Conformer model on GPU) emits partial transcripts continuously, so the final transcript is ready about 100–200 ms after speech ends.
The LLM (a small, fast model on vLLM, with the conversation prefix cached per call) starts generating immediately. Tokens stream out.
Streaming TTS starts synthesizing from the first sentence fragment. Audio frames go back over WebRTC.
Barge-in: when the user speaks, stop TTS playback and cancel the LLM generation instantly. The pipeline is orchestrated by LiveKit Agents or Pipecat.

sections.title: Latency budget
items: About 800 ms: VAD end-of-turn about 200 ms, ASR finalization about 100 ms, LLM TTFT about 200 ms, TTS first audio about 150 ms, network about 100 ms. Every stage must stream.

sections.title: Break it

cards.title: Serving a Giant Mixture-of-Experts Model
cards.subtitle: DeepSeek-V3/R1-class (671B total, ~37B active) at scale
cards.lego: A factory with 256 specialist builders where each brick is handed to only a few of them, so the factory is huge but each step is fast, as long as the hand-offs are quick.
cards.summary: Serve a 671B-parameter MoE model (256 routed experts, about 37B active per token) as a public API with high throughput per GPU. The model doesn't fit on one 8-GPU node in FP16, and expert routing creates all-to-all communication.
steps: Store weights in FP8 (about 700 GB). A prefill cluster and a decode cluster are sized separately (disaggregated), with KV transferred over RDMA.

Decode uses wide expert parallelism across many nodes (for example EP across 2–4+ nodes), so each GPU holds a few experts and gets large per-expert batches. Attention uses data parallelism to avoid duplicating KV.
All-to-all dispatch and combine of tokens to experts uses optimized kernels (DeepEP) and overlaps communication with compute (two-batch overlap).
An expert-parallel load balancer replicates hot experts on extra GPUs, because expert popularity is skewed and shifts with traffic.
Multi-token prediction heads serve as a built-in speculative drafter to boost decode speed. Prefix caching on disk or SSD serves repeated contexts.

sections.title: Why it's hard
items: Communication, not FLOPs, becomes the bottleneck. Interconnect topology (NVLink domain, InfiniBand or RoCE) decides the design.
Tiny per-expert batches waste GPUs, so wide EP needs lots of concurrent traffic to pay off.

cards.title: Multi-Region LLM API with Fallbacks
cards.subtitle: Capacity-aware global routing when GPUs are the scarce resource
cards.lego: Motor rooms in several cities: a dispatcher sends each job to whichever room has free motors, and to a rented room across town when all are full.
cards.summary: Run a company-wide LLM API across 3 regions with a 99.95% availability SLO. GPU capacity per region is fixed (reservations), traffic has daily peaks, and a region or an entire model pool can fail.
steps: Global DNS or anycast (Torbit or Cloud Load Balancing) sends users to the nearest healthy region's AI gateway.

Each gateway knows the real-time capacity of every region (queue depth, KV utilization, error rates) and spills over to another region when local pools are saturated. Streaming latency rises slightly; availability holds.
Priority classes: interactive traffic is served first. Batch and offline traffic go to a separate queue that absorbs idle capacity (off-peak) and is shed first under load.

The fallback chain per model: self-hosted primary, then a secondary region, then a smaller model, then an external vendor API (contractually approved), then a clear 'busy, retry later' with Retry-After.
The model registry and weights are replicated to every region (GCS multi-region or dual-region buckets). Rollouts go region by region, and SLO burn-rate alerts gate each step.

sections.title: Break it
items: Drain a whole region: the others must absorb the load. Plan N+1 regional capacity or accept shedding low-priority traffic.
A vendor fallback outage at the same time: the last line of defense is graceful degradation, not unbounded retries.

cards.title: Inline Safety & Moderation Guardrails
cards.subtitle: Classifiers on every prompt and response without doubling latency
cards.lego: Inspectors at both doors of the motor room who check every order coming in and every model going out, without making the line longer.
cards.summary: Every chat request and response for customer-facing LLM features must be checked for prompt injection, PII, toxicity and policy violations. Guardrails may add at most about 50 ms to TTFT and must scale with all LLM traffic.
steps: Input checks run in parallel with the start of generation: a fast PII detector plus a small injection and safety classifier (on Triton, or a Llama Guard-class model on vLLM). If a check fails, cancel the generation before anything reaches the user.
Output checks run on streamed chunks (every sentence or N tokens) so the stream isn't held until the end. Unsafe text is stopped mid-stream with a replacement message.
Deterministic rules (regex for card numbers, allowlists and blocklists) run first because they're cheap. Model-based checks come next. Only escalations go to a larger judge model asynchronously.
Violations and near-misses are logged to Kafka for review. Policies are versioned, and classifier updates go through shadow evaluation.

sections.title: Break it
items: The guardrail service is down: fail closed for high-risk features and fail open with extra logging for low-risk ones. Decide per feature in advance.

cards.title: Mini-MOC: Prefix-Aware Router vs Round Robin
cards.subtitle: Hands-on: prove why routing matters for LLMs
cards.lego: Run two dispatchers side by side, one random and one who remembers which builder has which pages open, and time them.
cards.summary: Run 2–4 small vLLM replicas (one GPU each, or CPU with a tiny model) and write a simple router in about 100 lines: hash the first N prompt tokens to a replica, with a load cap. Compare it against round robin on a chat workload with shared system prompts and multi-turn sessions.
steps: Generate a workload: 20 system prompts × 200 users × 5 turns, with each turn appending to the conversation.
Baseline: round robin via nginx or Envoy. Record TTFT p50/p95, the prefix-cache hit rate (vLLM metrics), and throughput.
Your router: consistent hashing on (system prompt plus session ID), falling back to the least-loaded replica when the chosen one's queue exceeds a threshold.
Bonus: try the Gateway API Inference Extension or llm-d's scheduler on kind or minikube and compare it with yours.
Write up the results: the hit-rate and TTFT improvement, and what happens when one replica gets a hot system prompt.

cards.title: Drill: Bad Model Rollout & Noisy Tenant
cards.subtitle: Chaos engineering for the model layer, not just the infrastructure
cards.lego: Slip a slightly miswired motor into the line and let one customer hog the dispatcher, then see whether anyone notices before the customers do.
cards.summary: Infrastructure is healthy, but the model is wrong: a new version that is 30% slower, emits malformed JSON 5% of the time, or has a broken chat template. Meanwhile one tenant sends 10× its normal traffic. Do your canaries, evaluations and quotas catch it?
steps: Hypothesis: the canary at 5% traffic detects the regression within 10 minutes and rolls back automatically, and other tenants' p95 TTFT stays within SLO during the noisy-tenant spike.
Deploy a deliberately degraded model version (a wrong quantization, a missing stop token, or a bad template) as the canary through the Istio or KServe traffic split.
Watch the signals: TPOT and TTFT per version, structured-output parse-failure rate, average output length (runaway generations), user thumbs-down rate, and guardrail triggers.
Simultaneously replay 10× traffic from one tenant key. Per-tenant token limits and fair queuing must contain it.
Record the time to detect and the time to roll back, and which dashboard or alert fired first. Add the missing ones.

sections.title: The lesson
items: Model regressions return HTTP 200. You need quality and behavior metrics per model version, not just error rates.

cards.title: Online LLM Serving Platform
cards.subtitle: Serve a 70B chat model to 10,000 concurrent users
cards.lego: The full motor room: front desk, smart dispatcher, racks of motor bricks, and gauges on every wall.
cards.summary: Design an internal platform serving open models (for example, a 70B instruct model plus an 8B) to many product teams with an OpenAI-compatible API, streaming, a p95 TTFT under 1 s, TPOT under 50 ms, per-team quotas, and cost efficiency.
steps: Clients call the AI gateway (auth, per-team token quotas, model routing, fallbacks, usage metering) behind Torbit or the CDN edge and Istio.
The gateway forwards to a Kubernetes inference gateway (GAIE or llm-d) whose endpoint picker scores vLLM or SGLang replicas on prefix-cache overlap, queue depth and KV utilization.

The 70B model runs in FP8 with TP=2 per replica on H100 or H200 nodes, with continuous batching, chunked prefill and prefix caching. At large scale, split into prefill and decode pools (disaggregation).
Weights come from the MLflow registry into GCS, and are cached on local NVMe or via GCS FUSE for fast cold starts. Images are pre-pulled on GPU node pools.
KEDA or HPA scales on queue depth and KV cache utilization, with minimum warm replicas. The cluster autoscaler adds GPU nodes, and GPU reservations cover the baseline.

Prometheus and DCGM track TTFT, TPOT, goodput, KV usage, GPU utilization and power. OpenTelemetry traces cover gateway → router → engine. Prompts and completions are logged to Kafka and the lake for evaluation.

sections.title: Capacity napkin
items: 10,000 concurrent streams at about 30 tokens/s each is 300k output tokens/s. If one TP=2 FP8 70B replica sustains about 3k tokens/s at the SLO, you need about 100 replicas (200 GPUs) plus headroom. Measure; don't guess.
KV cache: 70B with GQA (80 layers, 8 KV heads, 128 head dim, FP8) is about 160 KB per token, so a 4k context is about 0.65 GB per stream.

sections.title: Break it
items: Kill a GPU node mid-stream: clients get a retriable error and resume via the gateway retry. The router drains the dead endpoints.
A 100k-token prompt flood: chunked prefill or disaggregation protects the TPOT of other users, and gateway limits on max input tokens apply.

cards.title: Real-Time Recommendations
cards.subtitle: Feature store + two-stage retrieval and ranking + Triton
cards.lego: Grab a handful of likely pieces from a huge bin fast, then have an expert sort that handful into the perfect order, in under 100 ms.
cards.summary: Personalized product recommendations on the home page for 100M users, with p99 under 100 ms, reacting to clicks within seconds, and retrained daily.
steps: Clickstream goes to Kafka, then Flink computes real-time features (the last N items viewed, session category affinity) and writes them to the online feature store (Redis, Bigtable or Cassandra).
The nightly Spark batch computes long-term user and item features into the offline store, then materializes them online.
Retrieval: embed the user and run ANN search over item embeddings (vector DB or ScaNN/FAISS) to get about 500 candidates, plus rule-based candidates.
Ranking: fetch features for the user and candidates from the online store, then score them on Triton (dynamic batching, GPU), rerank for diversity and business rules, and return the top 20.
Log served features and outcomes to Kafka and the lake. Daily training with point-in-time joins, registered in MLflow, rolled out as a canary with an A/B test.

sections.title: Break it
items: The feature store times out: fall back to cached popular items (a degraded but fast default). The circuit breaker opens.

cards.title: Batch LLM Inference Pipeline
cards.subtitle: Ray Data + vLLM over 100M product descriptions
cards.lego: Run the motor room overnight on a giant pile of jobs: nobody is waiting for any single one, so pack the GPUs completely full.
cards.summary: Every week, generate enriched attributes and embeddings for 100M catalog items with an 8B LLM, maximizing tokens per dollar with no latency SLO, and write the results back to the lakehouse.
steps: Airflow triggers the job and reads a snapshot of the item table (Iceberg on GCS) with Ray Data, streaming in blocks.
CPU stages build prompts. GPU stages run vLLM engines as Ray actors (one per GPU) with large batches, prefix caching for the shared instruction, and FP8.
Use spot or preemptible GPUs with Ray task retries. Write output per block, idempotently, keyed by item ID.
Write results to an Iceberg table and publish a 'ready' event. The search index and feature store pick up the changes.

sections.title: Napkin
items: 100M items × about 300 tokens is about 30B tokens. At about 20k tokens/s per GPU for a batch-optimized 8B model, that's about 420 GPU-hours.

cards.title: RAG Shopping Assistant
cards.subtitle: Retrieval + LLM + guardrails
cards.lego: Before answering, the builder runs to the parts catalog, grabs the relevant pages, and builds the answer from them.
cards.summary: A chat assistant that answers product and policy questions grounded in the catalog and help-center documents, with citations, streaming, and under 2 s to first token.
steps: An offline pipeline (Airflow, Spark or Ray) chunks documents, embeds them, and indexes them into a vector DB plus a keyword index (hybrid search). CDC keeps prices and stock fresh.

Online: the AI gateway authenticates and applies guardrails, then query rewriting, then hybrid retrieval and a reranker, then a prompt with a stable system prefix (for prefix caching) plus the retrieved context.
The LLM is served on vLLM or SGLang behind the inference gateway. Responses stream via SSE with citations.
Log everything, run offline evaluations (groundedness, answer quality), and collect user feedback in MLflow and the lake.

sections.title: Break it
items: The vector DB is slow: time out and fall back to keyword search only. The LLM pool is saturated: queue with a clear message, or fall back to a smaller model.

cards.summary: Automate weekly retraining of a ranking model (or a LoRA fine-tune of an LLM) from fresh data, with evaluation gates, safe rollout and automatic rollback.
steps: The Airflow or Kubeflow pipeline builds a point-in-time training set from the feature store's offline store (Spark), pinned to an Iceberg snapshot.

cards.title: Mini-MOC: Serve & Benchmark a Model with vLLM
cards.subtitle: Hands-on: one GPU, one weekend
cards.lego: Build a small working motor yourself and put it on the test bench before designing the whole factory.
cards.summary: Serve a small open model (1–8B) with vLLM, or SGLang if you want to compare, on one GPU (cloud or local). Load-test it and plot how TTFT, TPOT and throughput trade off as concurrency rises.
steps: Run `vllm serve <model>` with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Scrape `/metrics` with Prometheus and graph it in Grafana.
Benchmark at concurrency 1, 8, 32, 128 (vLLM bench serve or a Locust script) with a fixed prompt and output length. Record TTFT, TPOT, tokens/s and KV cache usage.

cards.title: Drill: GPU Loss & KV-Cache Exhaustion
cards.subtitle: Chaos engineering for model serving
cards.lego: Pull a motor brick out while the machine is running, then overload the rest, and watch whether the gauges and dispatcher react in time.
cards.summary: Test that the serving platform degrades gracefully when GPUs disappear or the KV cache fills up, and that you see it coming on dashboards before users do.
steps: Hypothesis: losing one replica keeps p95 TTFT within SLO, and a traffic spike triggers queueing and scale-up, not errors.
Kill a vLLM pod or cordon a GPU node. The router must stop sending traffic to it within seconds, and in-flight streams must fail cleanly and be retried by the gateway.

Spike traffic with long prompts until KV cache usage reaches 100%. Watch preemptions, queue depth and TTFT. The autoscaler should fire on the queue metric, and the gateway should shed low-priority tenants first.
Check the alerts: KV cache above 90%, TTFT SLO burn rate, and GPU XID or DCGM errors. Record how long GPU scale-up really takes, from node to image to weights to ready.

sections.title: The lesson
items: GPU capacity is slow to add. Protect it with admission control and keep warm headroom, rather than relying on autoscaling alone.
